An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, when combining this result with the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ branching fraction, a 95% confidence level was achieved, resulting in an upper limit for the magnitude of the standard matrix element parameter $\Delta\Gamma_s$ at 0.021, which is the narrowest limit to date. Additionally, when assuming that the $B^0_s$ system follows a single-width scenario, a 90% confidence level was achieved, resulting in an estimation of the decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_s$ at -0.005 (with a 0.036) and a two-sided 90% confidence interval of -0.036 to 0.015. These outcomes, specifically the decay time and width difference, provide the most precise measures to date, with the results being consistent with theoretical predictions obtained through Lattice QCD calculations, which resulted in a decay time of 1.504 picoseconds and a two-sided 95% confidence interval for $\Delta\Gamma_s$ at -0.005 to 0.017. These outcomes further solidify the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time and width difference as critical parameters that will aid in constraining beyond-Standard-Model physics scenarios and refining the understanding of the $B^0_s$ system. Nonetheless, with an anticipated increase in available data to around 3 femtobarns, a projected threshold for the absolute value of $\Delta\Gamma_s$ could drop to 0.010 or lower. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The paper's initial section reviews the stochastic control problem and discusses the challenges associated with modeling the control variable's stochastic component. The subsequent section explores different numerical approaches, including a finite element method for solving the state equation and a Monte-Carlo method for the control problem. The paper concludes by examining the convergence properties of the numerical methods and discussing their practical applications. It also highlights the potential benefits of using a stochastic simulation technique for other similar mathematical problems. The numerical results presented demonstrate the method's effectiveness in solving the problem on a two-dimensional spatial domain with random input processes. The paper also compares the performance of the numerical method with respect to precision and computational time for different parameter settings. The numerical results confirm the method's ability to achieve accurate solutions for both small and large parameter settings, as well as its sensitivity to grid size, time step, and the number of Monte-Carlo simulations. The paper was originally presented at the 13th AOCMA conference held in Hanoi, Vietnam.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Specifically, we explore the possibility that quadrupolar components may be evident in smaller-scale anisotropy studies, and also consider the possibility that an incoming "neutron star wind nebula" may be influencing nearby cosmic ray flows. Finally, we suggest that a systematic re-analysis of extremely energetic cosmic ray data from other observatories may be worthwhile in order to further understand our findings. Additionally, we advocate for a significant expansion of ground-based cosmic ray detection facilities across the globe, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a deep understanding of ultra-high energy cosmic rays through direct detection. This, in turn, would allow for a richer interpretation of potential connections to nebulae and other astrophysical phenomena. This study's findings can be replicated by performing a re-analysis of the data, given access to the original raw data. The Anisotropy Code is available online at https://github.com/PAO-Antares/AnisotropyCode. The research reported here has been reviewed and approved by the Pierre Auger Collaboration. As such, it has not been assigned a Publication Number within the context of the Collaboration. The authors look forward to presenting this research for discussion and approval by the Collaboration in due course. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. The results of our analysis have provided valuable insights into the behavior of time series data and the effectiveness of the score-driven approach in modeling complex dynamics and forecasting such data sets. Our research has also been conducted using the RShiny framework to create an interactive visualization tool that enables users to explore and visualize the estimated time-varying parameters and forecast values for the specified data sets. This tool is available online at the specified URL.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. Using the EAGLE cosmological simulation, our findings of a moderate alpha-enrichment, nitrogen spread, and low s-process enrichment were replicated in a region with minimal star formation slowing, further supporting the estimated large distance of the cluster. The moderate metal content and unique chemical profile of Tononzintla 2 suggests a metal rich metallicity around solar values, likely formed during the collapse of a massive protogalactic cloud, consisting of several small, low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars, and a vast, metal-poor field. The distinctive features of this cluster provide a benchmark for identifying similar metal-rich globular clusters in the Milky Way, and the effects of massive protogalactic clouds on early star formation. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our results provided an alternative proof for the same-conditional almost sure convergence of the AMP algorithm in these models, as previously mentioned in lectures by Jean Barraug. It is worthwhile to note that our method may be applicable to an broader category of signals and models. Moreover, this technique helped us to obtain a more precise expression related to the efficiency of the AMP algorithm and facilitated an exploration of the AMP algorithm's performance in the "easy" regime. Moreover, our method may be an important contribution to an expanded discussion on the properties of the TAP free energy function and its relation to the ground truth energy function. It is also possible that our method may be applicable to an even broader category of signal detection models. Finally, our method may be an interesting approach to an investigation of the algebraic variational approximation method.

By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. These measurements enabled us to determine the optical system's performance in relation to the calibration of the atmosphere and implemented a technique to calculate the aerosol depth through a system's calibration of the spectrum. A data analysis method featuring precise calibration of the atmosphere was also developed to reduce uncertainties and improve accuracy. To further enhance accuracy, we developed an alternative method based on the spectral analysis of the data. Both methods showed similar results and similar levels of precision, ultimately achieving a precision of 0.01 without accounting for systematic errors. These methods can be applied to any astrophysical experiment using wide-field photometry and provide a practical solution for calibrating the atmosphere quickly, regardless of the availability of on-site absolute calibration systems. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenBerry/RefineRPN.

Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter at play. As such, further study is needed in order to allow a valid comparison of waveform patterns produced by simulations taking environmental factors into account, against their vacuum-based counterparts. Finally, the behavior of dense dark matter aggregates surrounding individual black holes, particularly in cases where the black hole has significant mass, is also being investigated. As expected, such systems exhibit irregular patterns, with oscillations that are influenced by the emission of gravitational waves. As for equal mass binary black hole systems, where matter aggregates surround both bodies, research suggests that, regardless of initial conditions, a state of convergence is reached, where both black holes orbit each other according to the established, long-lasting binary black hole profile, with no visible influence from the aggregate. It's also been found, through additional analysis, that if the mass of two binary black holes is significantly different, where one is roughly five times more massive than the other, for example, the behavior of surrounding dense dark matter effectively becomes similar to that of individual, massive objects, with irregular patterns and oscillations that are influenced by the emission of gravitational waves. It's also been found, through further simulation, with matter directly overlaid onto a binary system, without proper consideration given to potential environmental influences, artificial distortion results, rather than any sign of dark matter at play, and that such systems typically converge to established profiles over several orbits, with no visible influence from the aggregate, regardless of initial conditions, where systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Unlike current hybrid algorithms that may become trapped in local minima, our proposed algorithm uses a more efficient approach to solve these equations, allowing for a higher probability of reaching the optimal solution. Through simulations and real-world applications, our method demonstrates greater accuracy and efficiency when compared to other multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks. Specifically, our approach has a higher probability of achieving the optimal solution, as indicated by the Hamming distance and floating point value differences, and is particularly effective when dealing with smaller scale networks. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Experimental results show that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both subjective and objective evaluations on real-world images. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This involves utilizing the deformed Poisson brackets to derive 
a set of first-order differential equations, which can be solved to obtain the Dirac 
equation within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime. We provide an explicit example by solving 
a set of first-order equations in one dimension. We then extend this solution to the 
three-dimensional de Sitter spacetime and the de Sitter spacetime identified as the 
Schwarzschild black hole. We conclude by discussing the implications of this approach 
for solving the Dirac equation within the $n$-dimensional de Sitter spacetime. 

Keywords: $R$-Minkowski spacetime, de Sitter spacetime, deformed Poisson brackets, 
Schwarzschild black hole, conformally flat metric.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

Finally, we outline possible pathways for further optimizing performance and integrating more intricate security mechanisms. 

Our research, representing an early exploration of this concept, offers other researchers a starting point for continuing this investigation. 
Our hardware platform featuring multiple security-domains, where the limited amount of code running on each domain guarantees overall system security, can serve as a foundation for other projects. 
Our results demonstrating significant reduction in trust requirements for security applications and the related performance implications, can also provide guidance for other researchers in this field. 
Our OctopOS, the first operating system composed of several secure subsystems working together in distrust, can serve as both a model for other multi-domain hardware setups and a framework that can be adapted for use in other security-domain based hardware scenarios.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that a modest increase in training time allows the FPG algorithm to obtain robust policies comparable to those obtained in non-adversarial scenarios. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Notably, the orbital selectivity in cubanite can be modified by the intense optical transitions involving both atomic and molecular states, giving rise to potential applications in optoelectronics and medicine. Moreover, the presence of a dense 5d manifold is shown to influence the molecular and atomic orbitals, which in turn impacts the electron spatial segregation and optical transitions, potentially exploited in design of novel compounds. This study highlights the value of computational modeling in understanding the intricate nature of transition metal compounds and identifies cubanite as a promising material for further research into magnetic resonance and optoelectronics.

Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. Furthermore, this system provides a framework for investigating the interplay between multi-phonon states and the dark exciton energy structure. Lastly, the system's multi-phonon properties offer a potential solution to solve the bias ramping problem encountered in quantum accuracy metrology. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how bivectors can be utilized to develop a method for constructing specific types of gravitational field solutions directly from electromagnetic field data, given in the standard Minkowski space basis. This approach allows us to obtain the metrics corresponding to these solutions, given initially in the complex self-dual form, by implementing a backward projection from the complex null tetrad basis to the real basis in the Minkowski space. As a test of this approach, we generate specific examples of metric constructions for an arbitrary flat electromagnetic field with non-zero flux through a non-zero circle in the $x^1$-direction. Additionally, we examine the aspect of conformal flatness in relation to such solutions. As an analytical test, we construct metric configurations with non-zero, self-dual scalar fields, also expressed through the complex null tetrad basis. As an observational prediction, we derive an observable expression for the gravitational wave amplitude in the Blandford-Znajek mechanism. This expression is related to the accretion rate, spin parameter, and potential differences in the temperature of the horizons. We also explore the aspect of conformal flatness in this context, leading to proposed methods to improve theoretical models. We emphasize the significance of bivectors in relation to electromagnetic fields, particularly in situations where electromagnetic extraction plays a crucial role. We highlight the potential applications of this approach to enhance our understanding of high-temperature logarithmic corrections, photon polarization, and the conformal flatness aspect in accretion disks. We anticipate that implementing bivectors will enable direct construction of metric configurations for flat electromagnetic fields, facilitating the derivation of observable predictions in photothermal processes involving high-temperature logarithmic corrections. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. However, the method's ability to perform safely and efficiently relies on the correctness of the related Jacobian matrices. In some situations, the inability to form these matrices safely may cause the algorithm to become stuck in an iterative process. Nevertheless, the development of algorithms like LM-EnRML, along with its efficient implementation, enables it to be used as a model for enhancing other iterative methods that solve equations and handle uncertainty quantification. In addition, the inclusion of interface tools is necessary to make this method accessible to petroleum engineers, allowing them to easily incorporate it into the practice of well logging interpretation. In this study, we successfully incorporated the LM-EnRML method within an integrated well-logging interpretation workflow that was successfully tested against real data obtained from the North Sea. The accurate results obtained from this experiment confirm the effectiveness of this method in capturing related uncertainties, making it suitable for real-time geosteering. The inclusion of interface tools, along with the successful testing of the method against real data obtained from the North Sea, allows it to be made safely available to the community through an open-access protocol. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. All code and data used in this study are publicly accessible for replication and further research. It includes new adaptations not previously reported, such as adaptations to clinical notes and Wikipedia articles. Moreover, our proposed approach facilitates efficient decoding via two parsing strategies and showcases promising results on the LDC 2020 NER Challenge. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using this new method in relation to other approaches, including those requiring less computational resources, and provide location estimation with minimal interference in mind. This development holds significant potential for its application in tracking and location awareness in ZigBee networks. In addition, we observe that the new method achieves a notable reduction in average location estimation error when compared to other methods, especially in environments with high interference levels. Moreover, we find that the diversity measure provides a more reliable distance estimation than the mean, and incorporate this into our algorithm. Meanwhile, we investigate methods for calculating distance without extensive computational requirements, and include a comparison with highly complex methods, in the context of wireless sensor networks. This research has a potential to contribute to location awareness and tracking in ZigBee networks, and we express its value when computational resources are limited, and offer the code as a reference for further development. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By accelerating the development of multilingual models, we can better serve the needs of increasingly globalized communities. This work aims to spark conversation and guide research on NLP for societal good, specifically focusing on code-mixing between English and Hindi but with broader applications to other language combinations. This is achieved through an evaluation of existing work, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling four critical issues: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. Possible pathways are also outlined for developing necessary datasets, models, and technology to support this endeavor. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only populations living in large cities with diverse cultures managed to resist the spread of misinformation. Our findings suggest that combating online misinformation requires tailored approaches tailored to the unique characteristics of local communities. We also propose potential strategies for misinformation mitigation based on our results. We make all data and analysis code publicly available to facilitate further research into the dynamics of online misinformation dissemination. We introduce the Reddit News Dynamics Database, a comprehensive dataset that includes comment threads from the perspective of users with advanced features, addressing existing limitations in Reddit data access. We employ a highly efficient algorithm to identify relevant cultural and demographic characteristics from large populations based on small-scale, in-person experiments. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the circulation of news and misinformation in online communities, aligning with existing theories of culture and diffusion. We also conduct experimental research to validate our findings with physical experiments that mimic online interactions in a controlled environment. We analyze news articles that have been fact-checked by reputable organizations and found that only a minor fraction of misinformation originates from users, with the majority coming from credible news sources that have since been debunked. We recognize the limitations of relying on voluntary efforts from fact-checking organizations to mitigate online misinformation dissemination. We propose a potential solution by integrating a system of differentiated accounts that reflects user population characteristics, such as geography, culture, and diligence level, influencing the circulation of news articles, including misinformation, in online communities. This account system is susceptible to changes that occur during periodic elections, where users can vote for new features or update existing ones. We demonstrate the feasibility of this idea by developing a simple prototype and presenting the results of an experiment conducted on a large-scale Reddit dataset. The experiment returns a score that predicts the circulation of misinformation in various user populations

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code for HALFADO is openly available, providing a versatile detection framework that is adaptable to various applications and data streams. Furthermore, we include a set of pre-trained models for both of the scenarios mentioned above. HALFADO's code can be found at https://github.com/awasme/HALFADO. The project's website with further details is available at https://halfado.github.io/.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that speech content is relatively consistent across different vocabularies used by instructors, implying a potential for pre-defining the vocabulary taught to robots to facilitate learning. To further explore ways to enhance robotic learning through demonstration-based methods, possible strategies were proposed, including training speech recognition systems specifically for this purpose, integrating knowledge about speech variation, and developing more effective learning algorithms that can benefit from audio input from humans. Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Fisher information matrix, it's possible to estimate the measurement uncertainties $\sigma_M$ associated with detecting a hypothetical "Planet X" by analyzing its impact on the gravitational field of the known planets. Based on existing measurements from the Juno, Cassini, and Mars-orbiting spacecraft, a  statistical model forecasts a typical measurement uncertainty of $\sigma_M=0.22M_\oplus (d_x/400\,\textrm{AU})^3.$  Under ideal conditions, a  Planet X with mass five times that of the Earth at a distance of 400 AU can potentially be confirmed with certainty across the entire sky, whereas a  Planet X of the same size but located at 800 AU can be confirmed with the same level of certainty only over about 5% of the sky. The gravitational effect of an undiscovered Earth or Mars-mass object should be detectable for more than 90% of the sky up to 260 and 120 AU, respectively. Upcoming Mars ranging missions may provide slightly improved detection limits. The project also explores the effectiveness of highly accurate astrometry (determining positions and movements) of approximately 8000 Jovian Trojans from 2023 to 2035 using data from the upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).  It's determined that optical Trojan astrometry faces several dominant systematic errors which could potentially be addressed internally with little data loss, ultimately resulting in usable cross-checks with other ranging missions but no improvement in the optimal achievable values of $\sigma_M$ until Trojan data is at least 10 times more precise than expected. The most limiting factor in detecting Planet X through tidal gravitational field is actually the difficulty of differentiating it from the gravitational effect of the changing quadrupole moment of the Kuiper Belt as its objects orbit the sun. Nonetheless, it won't become the leading source of uncertainty until a substantial improvement in the current data is made. The project also considers various alternative approaches to detecting Planet X, including searching for signs of gravitational influence on the orbit of the Sun, looking for subtle patterns in the solar system's heliosphere, and directly observing the planet, but they all face significant challenges before they can match the sensitivity of the gravitational field method. The project also includes a simple global optimization technique that can significantly reduce the computational time required to analyze numerous combinations of parameters by narrowing them down to a more manageable range, ultimately requiring only a few orders of magnitude less than the standard method

Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/XLM-TM.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Nonetheless, we cannot confirm the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Additionally, we discovered that our findings rely heavily on the use of multivariate data analysis, and we recommend the incorporation of such techniques in future investigations. HawkingNet, along with the code used for our analysis, is available online for further exploration and potential improvements. Nevertheless, we cannot rule out the possibility that future analyses may uncover evidence supporting the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The holistic approach of MSDCR promotes a unified perspective on CDR, addressing data sparsity in domains and thereby empowering the vast range of applications fueled by recommender systems. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-VAI/tree/main/models/recommend/msdcr.

Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This study's outcomes highlight the complexities of developing scalable and dependable automated quality control pipelines for MRI data and emphasize the importance of thoroughly evaluating these methods across diverse, previously unseen data. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Building upon this finding, we propose that this strategic coordination between agents could serve as a basis for developing models of collective behavior in more complex systems. Furthermore, we suggest that systems exhibiting similar dynamics may exist in other contexts. Alongside discussing potential directions for future research, we also address potential limitations of the approach, such as the challenge of distinguishing between driving and controlled dynamics in complex systems. Through this work, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of the Motivation Dynamics framework and its scope, as well as the broader discussion on the application of low-dimensional modeling to analyze coordinated behavior in high-dimensional systems. Additionally, we hope to stimulate further investigation into uncovering underlying mechanisms driving observed patterns of collective action in complex systems. Alongside presenting the expanded Motivation Dynamics model, we also outline a new assessment tool aimed at evaluating the coherence of systems undergoing periodic changes, and showcase its utility through numerical data. This approach, alongside the emergence of a strange attractor in the multi-agent system, serves as the foundation for an ongoing discussion on the notion that cooperative behavior in complex systems may arise from the combination of persistent, cooperative interactions among agents in sensitive systems. Ultimately, we propose considering the possibility that underlying mechanisms driving coordinated behavior in such systems may rely on the activation of critical points in response to varying environmental conditions, and advance a hypothesis that this principle can be applied across a broad spectrum of complex systems. However, we acknowledge that this idea remains a subject for ongoing research and theoretical development. Through this work, we also address potential directions for further investigation, such as analyzing systems characterized by alternating patterns of cooperation and competition, as well as identifying methods to enhance the coherence of systems through targeted changes. Moreover, we propose considering the potential application of discrete mapping models to analyze coordinated behavior in high-dimensional systems, and discuss the challenge of distinguishing between driven and controlled dynamics in complex systems. Despite these challenges, we believe that exploring the Motivation Dynamics framework in a multi-agent context offers a valuable opportunity to contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving coordinated action in complex systems, and to stimulate further research into this topic. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Still, its utility will depend on the outcome of subsequent investigations into potential biases and limitations associated with this approach. Nonetheless, even without accounting for other external lensing effects, our method should be applicable to reduced datasets, such as those involving single, distant supernovae. As such, it could provide a means to obtain valuable insights into the properties of galactic haloes at the highest observable redshift ranges. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we established a framework to estimate the interaction strength between light and spin in these devices, showing that a large overlap between the optical transition and the spectral diffusion spectrum can result in significant effects. However, it's also possible to minimize these adverse consequences through careful selection of the device operation conditions. Ultimately, our study provides a foundation for evaluating the performance of silicon photon-spin interfaces based on T type damage centers and offers several approaches to optimize the operation of such devices. MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated processing techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into Automated Tumor Detection by comparing conventional image processing methods, such as morphological analysis and regional growth algorithms, in order to explore their application and effectiveness. A sample detection process is illustrated using a public dataset containing malignant brain tumors, and the results show that these conventional approaches can already achieve promising accuracy levels when proper parameters are optimized for each case. The findings highlight the potential for further improvement through the integration of radiologists' expertise and more efficient optimization methods in MRI tumor detection. Furthermore, the research identifies potential areas for enhancement in tumor segmentation, including the use of machine learning algorithms and multi-modal imaging techniques. Ultimately, this assignment aims to contribute to the development of automated tumor detection systems that can increase diagnostic efficiency and accuracy while also providing valuable insights for radiologists and healthcare professionals. This could ultimately lead to better patient outcomes through more targeted treatment plans. The proposed approach presents a foundation for, and sparks inquiry into, the broader implications of combining imaging data with sophisticated processing techniques, expert knowledge, and machine learning algorithms, and invites further exploration in this domain. The associated code for the comparative study between image processing methods has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach is an important step towards developing a machine learning model that can accurately remove the stellar activity from data sets and thereby detect exoplanets. This model is critical for undertaking large-scale analyses of low-mass stars like M dwarfs. Nonetheless, further research is needed to test the approach on a broader range of stars and to implement machine learning algorithms that can handle large data sets. If successful, this will unlock the full potential of studying exoplanets in this category.

This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a flexible and efficient data collection process in Wireless Sensor Networks, ensuring high reliability and performance. Firstly, a link quality estimation technique is utilized, enabling swift computation of link quality between nodes. Secondly, a hierarchical sector-based system is established to organize and coordinate nodes within each sector to minimize interference and improve data transmission. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated through a protocol, called HBCP, developed and evaluated in a simulated environment utilizing TinyOS and TelosB devices. The outcome of the evaluation revealed that HBCP can achieve very high reliability levels, particularly in large-scale networks and networks prone to bottlenecks. For example, a network of 100 nodes exhibited a reliable data collection rate of over 90%, while in smaller networks of 20 nodes this rate exceeded 99%. Furthermore, HBCP exhibited distinct advantages in reducing interference and the energy consumption per node. The evaluation also provided valuable data on the suitability of HBCP for large-scale networks and baseline reliability performance in comparison with standard BCP. The findings suggested that HBCP could serve as an innovative solution for link quality awareness in Wireless Sensor Networks. The implementation details and the code for the proposed methods are available for download at https://sourceforge.net/projects/hbcp/. In addition, the evaluation data and methodology can be found at https://sourceforge.net/projects/hbcp/threads/. For further information, please contact xia.zhang@utdallas.edu or zhangxia@sou.edu.cn. Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. We've established recently, much like our work on Deformed Special Relativity, that Fock's coordinate transformation can be developed from a novel, deformed form of the Poisson brackets.  Utilizing this approach, we successfully obtained the associated momentum transformation, which preserves the four-dimensional relationship between momentum and space, p_{\mu} x^{\mu}.  With the deformed algebra in hand, we derive the first Casimir invariant in this paper.  Following first quantization, we utilize the Klein-Gordon equation to show that Fock's spacetime corresponds to the de Sitter universe, whose spacetime radius can be defined by the invariant length representing the de Sitter hypersurface.  This result implies that Fock's spacetime is actually the (3+1)D representation of the four-dimensional de Sitter universe.  We then demonstrate that Fock's spacetime contains a compactified time dimension that can range from 0 to 2π, which is indicative of the cyclical cosmology proposed by Steinhardt and Turok.  Finally, we observe that Fock's spacetime can be viewed as the product of the real line and the circle S^1, whose topological structure is known as the solenoid, a concept that may offer a new perspective on the problem of time in quantum mechanics.  We also explore the potential for this approach to provide a new framework for monodromy problems and quantum mechanics on a curve.  With this work, we hope to have established a novel foundation for investigating fundamental issues in the context of Fock's spacetime.  We intend to delve deeper into these topics in future research. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address these challenges, we propose the use of adversarial techniques and neural networks for the purification of these distributions, enabling a more precise extraction of the implicit structure of word distributions. Our research paves the way for a deeper theoretical understanding of these models, as well as the exploration of related topics, such as the generation of synthetic texts. We publicly release all code, data, and adversarial models derived from our research, along with two novel datasets of finance-related text. We also introduce a standalone Python package called finance-text at https://github.com/AliAudit/finance-text. We hope this research facilitates the advancement of studies involving textual data in financial contexts. We also believe that our theoretical and practical contributions can be applied to other domains where deep learning Pitfalls might be experienced with word embeddings. We further propose the development of methods to present word distributions with multiple dimensions, such as polarized words, along with corporate names, along with the creation of multi-dimensional datasets, along with the generation of synthetic texts. We hope this research facilitates the advancement of studies involving textual data in financial contexts. We also believe that our theoretical and practical contributions can be applied to other domains

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, our data directly demonstrates the band folding in both superconducting and normal states around the zone center, allowing for correct assignment of the hole-like bands. Near the zone corner, our results show an electron-like and M-shaped band in both states and a superconducting gap size around the zone corner ($\sim$5.5 meV), contradicting previous findings. These outcomes reveal a new gap structure around the zone corner, resolve prominent controversies and offer novel perspectives to analyze and understand the mechanism behind superconductivity in iron-based superconductors.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints. This equivalence is demonstrated for both rotation-invariant and orthogonal-invariant matrix ensembles, and it is suggested that this equivalence holds universally for any rotation-invariant matrix ensembles. Furthermore, practical applications of this equivalence have been illustrated through the calculation of supersymmetric matrix integrals related to the Gaussian free field, and the corresponding correlation functions for complex zero modes have been derived. Additionally, we explore the connection between these strategies and the superbosonization formula within the context of orthogonal-invariant matrix ensembles. Lastly, we highlight the importance of establishing this equivalence for supermatrix calculations, and we anticipate that this development will facilitate the introduction of orthogonal-invariant supersymmetry, enabling the study of systems involving interlocking modes, such as clock waves and quasi-zero modes in the harmonic map matrix ensemble.

Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This analysis's capabilities to differentiate between the standard model and certain 
exotic top quark scenarios in $t$-channel single top quark production, specifically 
exotic polarization and scalar-glue-disk models, have also been outlined. 
These new results build upon previous research conducted at the Tevatron and LHC. 
The most sensitive parameter settings for the spin asymmetry observable have been 
determined, which involves combining the results from multiple angular observables. 
The study of the spin asymmetry in $t$-channel single top quark production has the 
potential to contribute significantly to the discovery potential of several new 
physics scenarios in future experiments with higher luminosity and energy. 
For the LHC with 13 TeV and a total luminosity of 300 fb^-1, it is anticipated 
that the spin asymmetry observable will be sensitive to an integrated cross-section 
times polarization of 1.03 to 1.53 pb, which is relevant to the $t$-channel 
single top quark production of exotic top quark scenarios. 
Furthermore, with 8 TeV data and a total luminosity of 100 fb^-1, it is expected 
that the spin asymmetry observable will be sensitive to an integrated cross-section 
times polarization of 0.40 to 0.63 pb.

standard model and the complex scalar top partner model type I,

Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Additionally, we obtained the spin-spin interaction and shift spectra, providing further insight into the microscopic structure and dynamics of LaNiO$_3$ within the superlattices. Our findings demonstrate that LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices exhibit the same correlated metallic state regardless of LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, as demonstrated by the linear increase of the spin-lattice relaxation inverse proportionally to temperature in all cases. This suggests that a minimum amount of correlation exists between the motion of electrons within LaNiO$_3$ layers even when they are separated by a single LaAlO$_3$ layer. This is consistent with the previous prediction that a continuous band of charge carriers forms at the LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ interface. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our findings demonstrate significant 
improvements over baseline generators in terms of conversational quality and 
efficiency, supported by detailed analysis of our datasets and evaluation 
methods. Our code and datasets are available for public access at our website. 
Our research offers numerous potential applications and invites further 
investigation into conversational dialogue generation. In the process, we 
developed an innovative assessment of diversity that can be applied to other 
generative models as well. 

Keywords: conversational dialogue, tree-structured data, automatic evaluation, 
text generation, dialog management, graphical models, multi-agent systems, mixed 
initiative interactions, intelligent interfaces, human-computer interaction.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys.
