By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. The high requirements for measuring this transition are due to the need for very strong magnetic fields that can override the material's normal point of high singularity, and the fact that the rotation of the lattice structure occurs over a narrow range of magnetic fields and temperatures. The discovered phase shift provides clear evidence for the $d$-wave nature of the superconducting gap in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. In addition, this research has the potential to contribute to the development of various surface-sensitive techniques that utilize depth sensing and could benefit from brush geometry calculations. In particular, we propose the utilization of curved brush models in relation to the Elneview method, a theoretical analysis that could facilitate the deconvolution of depth-sensing data in light scattering experiments used to analyze brush geometry. This study offers a significant theoretical framework that can serve as a reference for further research on curved brush surfaces and make a practical contribution to the improvement of light scattering analysis techniques used to study brush geometry. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, this method allows for more realistic simulations of the telescope and detector, which can be used to model biases and counting statistics, thereby producing more accurate predictions of the spectral characteristics of these sources. This methodology is openly available for the community to utilize and incorporate into their analyses. Alongside this, they also introduce the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope largest release of data, the High Energy All-sky Resolution Survey (HEARS), which comprises deep-field and wide-area observations, totaling about 7 years of data. HEARS includes various novel products, such as energy spectra and light curves for each source, and is accessible through the HEARS catalog, a massively multi-TB catalog containing over 5 million sources. This catalog is the most comprehensive release of data for the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to date, and is ready for use by the scientific community through the HEARS website. This strategy for machine learning-based image processing of space telescope data, along with the HEARS catalog, is hoped will inspire a broader adoption of these algorithms and advance the field of gamma-ray astronomy. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We provide concrete examples and empirical evidence showing that our proposed action sequences result in acceptable social welfare in various applications, including those mentioned above. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and examine the combinatorial optimization challenges in relation to the price of serial dictatorship. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to a better understanding of the capabilities and limitations of the serial dictatorship mechanism in combinatorial optimization contexts. We have also made theoretical and practical improvements, also anticipating these will spark further research in this field. We have implemented our solutions and associated algorithms and are prepared to accommodate open research and collaborative efforts in this area. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From a total of 4575 selected targets, our analysis identified 29 
binary prospects, including 11 previously unknown wide binary asteroids. One
of these newly discovered asteroids, named 2014 OS389, features a 36 kilometer 
primary component with a 13 kilometer secondary, orbiting at a distance of 41 
astronomical units with a highly eccentric 440 day period. This find highlights
the capabilities of the proposed detection method and suggests that detecting 
wide binary asteroids is feasible with current wide field surveys. However, it 
is also clear that the vast majority of detected binary prospects will prove 
incorrect, necessitating the implementation of an efficient and reliable 
validation process to accurately validate genuine binary cases. We outline 
and executed validation criteria involving a combination of optical astrometry
and the characteristics of the asteroid's orbit, resulting in 11 previously unknown
wide binary asteroids and confirming one more, with all discovered targets 
meeting the defined orbital stability standards. These findings significantly 
expand the known roster of wide binary asteroids. Meanwhile, 2014 OS389, with 
its substantial dimensions and highly eccentric orbit, presents an intriguing
opportunity to test binary stability constraints and test mass inferences based 
on the existing record of single asteroid measurements. Furthermore, it provides
an ideal target for studying binary cohabitation through optical astrometry and
radiometric analysis, as well as for scheduling future

interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,

processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user
interactivity. Additionally, the adoption of modern web frameworks facilitates
extensive customization, making our visualization tools effortlessly integratable
into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is
also compatible with Aladin Lite and other popular third-party web tools. We've

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This is evident in structural styles, isostatic equilibrium, rock types formed and geochemical fingerprints.  This research's approach provides a new methodology for analyzing and modeling the evolution of rifted passive margins.  It offers a framework for investigating the effects of geodynamic process on the development of rifted passive margins.  It also enables the prediction of conjugate margin evolution based on analysis of already broken-up margins. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we uncover that incorporating a Dopamine-like value estimation method amplifies the benefit, while we also identify challenges posed by the complex, multi-turn nature of these conversations. Our success paves the way for future D&D challenges centered on natural language understanding, as we make the code and data available at: https://github.com/hahnfrt/dotproduct-dnd. Human evaluations, alongside the code and data, are incorporated within our supplementary materials, which is accessible at: https://github.com/hahnfrt/dotproduct-dnd/tree/main/supplements. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. In contrast to previous studies, our work relies on robust, statistically significant results rather than model-based assessments. The discovered new words and their meanings have been verified against existing lexical resources, revealing both previous model assessments and expert knowledge onto often align. For the primary dataset employed, our method recovers a significant proportion of the true positives (75%) and excludes the majority of negatives (91%), indicating its effectiveness in both change discovery and reduction of theoretical type spaces. Further development of more accurate change detection models is anticipated to enhance discovery accuracy. The proposed framework is available online.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This study demonstrates that the folding of proteins with trefoil knots relies on local transitions and initial knot placement, and that deeper knots may face challenges due to pressure from inward looping segments. Our analysis also identifies two key patterns in protein geometry with shallow knots, and suggests that folding laws for knotted proteins can be derived from the properties of free knots. By exploring the connections between free-knot placement and protein folding, our research provides insights into the intricate processes of protein folding and may help develop new indicators for assessing protein structures and predicting their folding pathways. Furthermore, our study introduces knotoids, a statistical framework that can be applied to analyze other complex structures, such as those found in viral capsids, DNA, and RNA. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a comprehensive understanding of protein geometry and its related folding challenges. As such, it is hoped that this study will spark collaborative efforts among physicists, biologists, and mathematicians to uncover the intricate secrets of protein folding. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. Although the hypothesis remains an open question, some of the proposed formulas to estimate the non-zero values of energy levels in Heisenberg algebra are determined. Additionally, the anomalous NG theorem has been shown to imply the non-integrability of some Heisenberg algebra systems. Consequently, systems with an anomalous NG mode may not have a finite number of conserved quantities. Instead, they only possess a continuous number of conserved currents derived from the Heisenberg algebra itself. In conclusion, this research has demonstrated that both the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem and the resulting Heisenberg algebra, which generates mass within the NG sector, can be understood through the lens of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Moreover, the relationships between the Anomalous NG theorem, the Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector have been established.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, we observe that these improvements translate to real-world applications, yielding a 2% enhancement in semantic similarity and a 10% improvement in textual classification when aided by this counterfactual data. The code and data developed as part of this research are now available for public access at https://github.com/google-research/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. A theoretical model indicated that strain from the epitaxial relationship can significantly strengthen the spin-orbit coupling in LaPtSb, located near a quantum point where its spin-orbit coupling is weak. This could make this material an appealing candidate for spin-orbit coupled effects, given the right epitaxial growth conditions. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the successful growth of highly lattice-mismatched Heusler compounds on clean graphene substrates, offering a foundation for investigating their unique electronic properties. Furthermore, it provides concrete evidence for a remote epitaxial process, and highlights the importance of careful contamination control and surface diffusion consideration for this technique. It also suggests that strain from epitaxial relationships may be utilized to manipulate the spin-orbit coupling in materials. Finally, it suggests that suitable annealing procedures and precise consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are essential for achieving desired epitaxial relationships with a range of materials, and that a 30 degree rotation domain percentage is a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This study's findings demonstrate its relevance to the broader agenda of developing new materials through the synthesis of composite superlattices and multilayers on clean graphene substrates. Finally, it's expected that the experimental evidence for remote epitaxy presented in this study will stimulate the development of new theoretical models describing the underlying physics of this process. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  Moreover, the technique proves particularly beneficial for GANs trained on datasets with limited annotation. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. We also found a clear distinction between our scores for low and high levels of excess returns, providing early evidence of the practical value of our method. However, it is necessary to deepen understanding of the cross-sectional returns and the scoring system to fully utilize the computational tools developed here. The code is available online for further exploration and improvement. Despite its simplicity, our approach offers a robust foundation for modeling portfolio returns and may be a useful starting point for more advanced research algorithms. It is also possible to adapt our score-based approach to other types of investments beyond the long-only strategy. Consequently, our research provides a stepping stone for investigating fundamental questions in finance, such as the relationship between returns and the cross-sectional distribution. Ultimately, answering these fundamental questions is crucial for developing effective research algorithms and making informed investment decisions. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The source code for FedHealth is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can access it at the following address: https://github.com/alexfeng95/FedHealth. You can also reach the corresponding author at afeng95@umich.edu for additional information.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in efficient learning for temporal sequences. Compared to conventional techniques, incorporating simultaneous supervised learning and metric adaptation enhances prediction accuracy in both synthetic and real-life scenarios, according to our results. Furthermore, the features identified by relevance learning show impressive comparisons to those of alternative methods. Additionally, our method allows for the visualization of low-dimensional grid data, highlighting the temporal structure in the data. Moreover, pruning of irrelevant dimensions provides a score for each dimension, offering a quantitative understanding of the data and guiding experimental design in subsequent studies. Ultimately, our approach facilitates the exploration of complex temporal sequences through its interactive three-dimensional plots. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
This research also involves an open question regarding the sequence reconstruction
problem that was initially posed by Levenshtein. 
It concerns the question of whether a particular number, that is equal to the least
common multiple of the number 5 and any other number, can be expressed as a product
of two distinct factors that are greater than 2 and where these factors are of the same
type as the factors of the number 5, namely odd primes. 
This question has since been answered in the affirmative for all numbers that are greater
than 5, but we decided to maintain the original formulation of this question as it was
initially posed to us by Levenshtein. 
We also provide examples of the sequence reconstruction problem that are of general interest. 
Additionally, we offer the Cayley graph, its description and the specific distance metric
it uses, but we believe that this graph warrants further study in its own right.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This technique also allows a notable expansion of the number of classes that can be learned without a significant increase in learning difficulties. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The code, data, and experiments are available at https://github/qasper.

The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. This framework is made feasible by the low eccentricity approximation leading to highly consistent results with existing searches, specifically for narrow-band searches and certain wide-band searches, whereas it facilitates further search strategies within the NGBE regime. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, researchers, policymakers, and analysts must closely collaborate to develop, fit, and utilize models in a way that accurately reflects the complex interplay between viruses, hosts, and their environment. Ultimately, this collaboration is crucial for mitigating the consequences of pandemic epidemics and potential future outbreaks.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the non-adabatic case, we derived a complex quantum pendulum model that includes multiple pendulum-like motions and quantum spin-molecule atom interactions, resulting in the possibility of both stability and large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In scenarios where the dark state condition is not met, we found an interactive quantum pendulum model where quantum rotations and pendulum-like movements combine with quantum molecule-atom interactions, resulting in both stable and large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In all situations, we offer possible experimental signatures and related theories. In addition, our work offers novel perspectives on quantum pendulum theory and may enable the creation of molecule-atom pairs through three-body interactions in spin-unit systems. In systems without spin units, however, this process appears highly challenging. In such cases, alternative approaches based on dark state conditions in suitable collisions and light-based association, such as spin-changing collisions and Feshbach association, may be necessary. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This includes the need for more versatile theories capable of analyzing nodal lines in artificial materials composed of multiple bands, as well as the difficulty of reliably detecting the topological nature of artificial nodal lines. This review is accompanied by an original appendix that presents a model exhibiting both a topological nodal line and a nodal point. This model involves artifical magnetic atoms placed on a triangular lattice and is capable of being experimentally realized using ruby ruby-based artificial lattices filled with a strong magnetic field. This framework offers a platform for testing the novel properties associated with topological nodal lines in artificial materials. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Experimental results show MAG-Net's high accuracy in tumor type classification and segmentation, demonstrating its potential as a reliable AI model for brain tumor diagnosis and treatment planning.  The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashish411/MAG-Net.  The study's findings contribute to the development of more effective brain tumor diagnosis models and provide a foundation for extending the model to other medical applications.  The developed code is versatile and adaptable for use with other segmentation tasks at https://github.com/ashish411/MAG-Net#mag-net-for-segmentation.  The project includes a demonstration of the model's performance on the ISBI Brain MRI Segmentation Challenge 2020 dataset.  The study's code and results can be accessed on Figshare at https://figshare.com/projects/Multi-Task-Attention-Guided-Net-MAG-Net/19921.  The research is contributed to the Brain Tumor Image Segmentation (BRAIN) Challenge 2021 and the ISBI Brain MRI Segmentation Challenge 2020. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this framework offers a way to learn optimality criteria for shadow optimization, enabling the efficient generation of synthetic shadows for various tasks, such as lighting design, shadow manipulation, and illuminating multiple objects. By demonstrating both explicit and implicit rendering implementations, as well as qualitative and quantitative evaluation of our method, we show its effectiveness and efficiency in computing accurate shadows, even when incorporating learned optimality criteria, and highlight its potential for shadow-based inference and learning. The code is available at https://github.com/ninghang/ShadowOpt.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. The proposed system has particular applications in the post-production industry, where it can be incorporated into non-linear video editing software to provide a range of options for regenerating missing scan lines. This allows editors to balance visual clarity with playback smoothness in just a few adjustments. This research also lays the groundwork for the exploration of other interlacing-related problems. The proposed system and test data are made publicly available to facilitate future research in this area. Experimental results validate the uniqueness of the proposed approach, and the code and data can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/zyang0126/Interlacing-ICME2020. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass. The ratio of the neutron skin thickness to the neutron radius was calculated and proposed as a more robust parameter to investigate in experiments. Additionally, predictions were made for various isotopes of lead and mercury. The results highlighted the importance of distinguishing between the radius of the point neutron distribution and the neutron skin thickness, especially if future experiments aim to test the Caesarian theorem through measurements of nuclear radius and bulk properties. Lastly, the study suggested that the introduction of finite density self-constant relativistic mean field models may be necessary to accurately interpret such data.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Notably, our SVE model exhibits higher precision and efficiency than the PCA-DNN and SE models. The associated latency and accuracy improvements have significant implications for the development of real-time flood risk management systems. In addition, this research is made more actionable by incorporating the predictions in a risk management policy, demonstrating the potential for such models to inform decision-making processes. Ultimately, this work highlights the potential of machine learning algorithms to tackle complex hydrodynamics problems, while also addressing data availability challenges. As such, this research provides a theoretical foundation for exploring other practical applications of these fast solver models, such as predicting ocean flow velocities. As numerical solver methods continue to evolve, there is a clear potential for this model to be adapted for use with other partial differential equations. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. This approach also offers a potential solution to the challenge of scaling up catalytic reactor design. Reply to comments from reviewers is included in the appended file. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Findings reveal that the BDDC algorithm is highly effective, requiring only one percent of the total memory to solve the system, and demonstrating robustness in responding to changes in tissue mechanical properties, finite element grid resolution, and the presence of infarced regions within the heart muscle. Moreover, the project showcases the capabilities of contemporary high-performance computing technology to efficiently solve computationally intensive cardiac mechanics problems, making way for realistic parameter scans that can inform clinical research and medical procedures. The scalable solution-building approach used in this research can also be applied to other complex medical applications. The implementation details, including the solution algorithm and cardiac mechanics theory, are outlined in the accompanying full paper. The BDDC algorithm code is now publicly available as part of the BelLCecI package on the NetNLC web site. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. This, in turn, provides valuable insights into the inherent properties of neural networks in relation to adversarial robustness. As a result, our proposed metrics can serve as invaluable tools for developers aiming to enhance the adversarial robustness of neural networks. This research is particularly relevant to the ongoing debate surrounding the efficacy of adversarial training, a widely adopted defense mechanism. Our findings, obtained by applying our metrics to various models, including a comprehensive analysis of adversarial training with different training periods, have significant implications for the field. This study is now available on arXiv, with a companion code repository available on GitHub. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This breakthrough paves the way for optimizing microacoustic structures for specific applications and fabricating complex acoustic metagratings in the MHz frequency range. This represents a significant advancement for ultrasound imaging and could also lead to further innovations in acoustic manipulation.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, rigorous evaluation shows that EBOS achieves notable gains in tuning both test accuracy and uncertainty, achieving robust performance across diverse dataset combinations. With straightforward integration into existing classifier architectures, our pioneering work lays the foundation for continuous exploration of open-world modeling in deep neural networks. Implementations and further findings are available at https://github.com/hjdw/EBOS.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Additionally, this novel SPADE scheme may be applied to the efficient collection of bi-photon pairs separated in frequency, thereby enabling the realization of quantum imaging based on bi-photon interferometry. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. It includes a summary of the work of Scheja and Tsuji, detailing how Hodge-theoretic obstructions can be used to construct and show geometric properties of compactifications via mirror symmetry, specifically for the case of blow-ups of projective spaces. A final section outlines potential directions for further research and related open questions. By doing so, this write-up aims to make the existing work of Scheja and Tsuji accessible, while also exploring the broader implications and opportunities within this field.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Furthermore, the composition of the 'inner' and 'outer' trajectories provides insight into the prevalence of the two species of predators. The methods employed in this analysis are applicable to other systems with singular perturbations and multiple time scales. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The evaluation shows that, depending on the specific program and protocol in question, successful verification and optimal fence placement can be achieved in a reasonable time. Nonetheless, there are cases where the protocol's memory reordering nature leads to an infinite number of possible program states, forestalling verification. Moreover, some programs have been found where optimal fence placement results in no visible performance difference compared to the original protocol. Despite this, the study reveals that the coherence mechanism's influence on memory access ordering gives rise to additional reordering opportunities, thereby improving program performance. Ultimately, the research uncovers that, when combining this mechanism with other ordering mechanisms, the resulting programs can exhibit greater order complexity. The associated code reordering patterns have been identified and classified, yielding a set of fundamental patterns that underpin all other derived patterns. The analysis also uncovers the existence of counter-example paths, enabling fence insertion, as well as the existence of program states that can comply with safety criteria despite employing the coherence protocol. Moreover, the study reveals that, when considering the coherence mechanism in isolation, the complexity of order complexity theory reduces from N^2 to N. The research further proposes a theoretical approach to optimizing fence cost, involving the employment of a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure. The proposed method involves the sequential application of fence insertion operations across all counter-example paths. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. As a significant aspect of this project, all design files and software are available for public reproduction, offering a valuable teaching tool that can help students thoroughly understand the operation and design of content-addressable processors. The CAPP's potential as a modular building block for a large-scale CSA system is also briefly explored. The research team successfully executed various algorithms and operations on the CAPP prototype, including lookup, parallel write, value merging, counting, and bit manipulation, and has openly shared the test data and performance metrics associated with these experiments. As the first public hardware reproduction of a Caxton C. Foster's content-addressable parallel processor design, this project marks an important milestone in the evolution of CAPP concepts and serves as a springboard for further discussions on the feasibility of large-scale content-addressable systems. The reproduced CAPP can be employed in various applications, such as automated theorem proving, pattern recognition in artificial neural networks, and high-performance computing tasks like database queries. Furthermore, the team suggests that the CAPP's circuit architecture may be adapted to develop an innovative cryptographic device capable of rapid data encryption. As the first open reproduction of a Caxton C. Foster's content-addressable parallel processor design, this project provides the underlying hardware, associated software, and performance metrics that validate its operation, and is now available for the public to reproduce and further develop. The design files and associated software can be found on the associated GitHub repository. The content-addressable parallel processor has been successfully executed on an Xilinx XC2S100 FPGA using the Xilinx ISE 14.2 and was developed using the Xilinx FPGA development board and supplied by the University of Hertfordshire. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. Our research provides a novel perspective on the evolution of galaxies at $\rm z\approx3$, involving a interplay between core and disk components, influenced by galaxy-building mergers and accretion streams. This could result in quenching, as seen in these galaxies, as well as the construction of bulges. This phenomenon may repeat itself in a cycle of merger-building, followed by a major collision. This is accompanied by a substantial bulge construction, followed by a quiescent galaxy appearance, until that collision occurs. We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass characterizing ratio observables, that could be probed via oscillations, beta decay, and cosmological processes. Consequently, our revised analysis significantly surpasses the initial analysis and confirms that the UTZ theory remains a coherent and compelling flavour theory. The findings also highlight the capability of robustly assessing multi-parameter flavour models with MCMC techniques. Nonetheless, the interpretation of our results is complicated by the presence of certain solutions that, although statistically significant, lack a clear theoretical basis. Consequently, we propose a method to distinguish physically meaningful solutions from other options. We also introduce a new criterion to select a single preferred solution that can be tested experimentally, in contrast to the existing variant of the UTZ model. Moreover, we present revised predictions for the mass ratio $\frac{m_2}{m_3}$ and the sum of neutrino masses $\sum m_\nu$, and predict that the UTZ model can explain the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon, with a magnitude consistent with observed values. Finally, we anticipate that the revised analysis will contribute meaningfully to further experimental and theoretical research into the UTZ flavour model. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure. Furthermore, we observe our approach succeeds where other methods fail, and analyze our findings based on generated code examples. The method's source code is available at https://github.com/fuji-sdl/CodeGS. We also introduce a new challenge evaluating generator quality through the extent of code they can generate, and present our approach as a starting point for future research and enhancement. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. Our study demonstrates that our quantum-inspired method not only achieves comparable performance to other methods but also excels in streaming environments characterized by gradual changes, yielding similar or better results with substantially fewer updates. Moreover, our approach boasts exceptionally low memory usage and similar or better predictive capabilities when tested on static versions of the data sets.
