A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Conversely, we arrive at an existing conclusion about compelled multifactor authentication, yet our framework offers a fresh perspective on the issue. Lastly, we conclude that even if compelled decryption is not actable, the respondent can still be compelled to provide access to their device, a notion we find counterintuitive. Ultimately, we believe our framework provides a language that is conducive to engaging in the broader debate about compelled actability, and we look forward to participating in this discussion with experts in the field. This paper's innovative contribution will serve as a starting point for a more extensive exploration of the issue, rather than a definitive conclusion, in the hope that it will spark a thorough examination of compelled actability in cryptography. In particular, we hope to explore how our framework can be applied to compelled cryptography in an experimental setting, such as part of a field trial or an actual court case. Additionally, we wish to develop a larger theoretical framework that can be used to evaluate the compelled actability of various cryptographic tools, including those that cannot be directly applied in a real-world setting. Furthermore, we believe it is essential to undertake a broader examination of the issue, one that considers both the theoretical and applied aspects of compelled actability in cryptography. In this context, we invite experts in the field to join us in this endeavor, contributing their insights and helping us develop a more comprehensive understanding of this complex issue. Ultimately, we believe that this discussion will yield a more coherent and unified approach to addressing the compelled actability

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. With a mass of 1.47 ± 0.08 solar masses, KIC 9267654 is the most massive star thus far subject to detailed internal rotation analysis, and it presents an compelling case for further examination in the field of astrophysics. Despite being a relatively short baseline, we were also able to monitor the star's internal rotation rate changes over a 4-year period, but no significant variations were observed. Through radial velocity measurements, we discovered that the star exhibits a modest eccentric orbit, but no significant impacts were found on its internal rotation profile. Lastly, we expanded our analysis to include three additional low-mass giant stars, Suyama's sample, and compared the stars' internal rotation profiles. Although KIC 9267654's unique internal rotation pattern may be an unusual case, we believe it is worthwhile to follow this star and its counterparts in the future to better understand its internal dynamics. With nearly four years of data available, we are already seeing the benefits of combining solar-like oscillations with other observational and theoretical studies of these interesting stars. In the field of low-mass giant stars, this strategy has the potential to advance our understanding of angular momentum conservation and the internal structures of these stars. In the longer term, answering these questions will provide valuable insights into the development of these stars throughout their main sequence phase. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's capability to handle emerging events has been successfully evaluated using a newly proposed metric called the Average Performance on New Events (APNE). The meta-based approach developed in this research achieves a notable improvement of over 10% in accuracy when applied to newly emerging events. The comprehensive experiments conducted demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems. Finally, we conduct numerical analyses to present results for M/M/1/1 and M/G/1/1 queues.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Furthermore, a short circuit method is presented to generate GCA in any desired dimension from existing lower-dimensional GCA, enabling the creation of GCA in extremely high dimensions. Lastly, a method linking GCA and tight frame coherence leads to a proposal to explore the properties and construction of GCA in the context of Euclidean space. Which, in turn, may contribute to further research in the field of channel estimation and signal detection.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

These proposed protocols improve previously known protocols and determine the minimum entanglement cost required to locally distinguish these UPBs. This research therefore provides new constructions of UPBs with strong quantum nonlocality, as well as new entanglement-assisted local distinguishability protocols with optimal entanglement costs. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn appears to be directed towards the supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center, enhancing the merger-driven starburst. Furthermore, we observed a higher percentage of active supermassive black holes (75%) during late stages of merger, in contrast to active galactic nuclei (50%) and low levels of supermassive black hole activity (30%) observed at early stages of merger. These findings are consistent with the prediction that supermassive black holes play a critical role in absorbing the energy of galaxy mergers, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. These results also indicate that active supermassive black holes play a key role in suppressing the outflow of gas, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our experiment employs a variety of evaluation metrics to compare the performance of multiple NN models, yielding a classification accuracy of 75% on the test data. 
This work's contributions lie in both the introduction of the RFS dataset and the effective use of data augmentation to achieve precise weather classification. 
The code and dataset are available for download at the specified link. 
The proposed algorithm's code has been successfully integrated into the PyTorch library. 
Alongside the introduction of the RFS dataset, our research provides an analysis of diverse weather conditions represented by images, and the code for the proposed algorithm has been successfully implemented using PyTorch. 
In the future, this dataset can be combined with datasets from other geographic locations to create a unified dataset for weather classification. 
Additionally, further research is anticipated to tackle the challenge of labeling semi-supervised weather condition images.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code will be made available on the GitHub repository specified in the paper.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts. It is predicted that future observations of cluster sizes and shapes, such as those planned with the Square Kilometre Array, could distinguish between these cosmologies by analyzing the evolution of cluster sizes and shapes up to $z \approx 1$.$\backslash$linebreak The method also enables the assessment of the effectiveness of various structure formation codes in mimicking the behavior of actual cosmological simulations. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. The proposed model also offers novel insights into the fundamental structure of atmospheric convection. Through the incorporation of a relatively simple closure mechanism inspired by the Phillips (1972) prescription, the model successfully replicates the celebrated $R^{\beta}$ scaling relationship renowned in the study of convection. The analytical model exhibits negligible computational burden, making it suitable for direct integration into full-scale atmospheric and climate models powered by the Euler equations. The success of this two-fluid model serves as a timely reminder of the value of drawing analogue insights from the study of convection in dense fluids and Rayleigh-Benard convection in the exploration of atmospheric convection. The model is also available in a user-friendly code format on established repository services. The ultimate goal of this research remains the development of a multi-fluid model that can adaptively adjust the number of active fluid components based on local turbulence characteristics for enhanced simulation performance. Nonetheless, the present two-fluid model represents an important initial step towards this objective. The proposed approach has been positively received by multiple leading researchers in the field, who are now incorporating their own variations of this model into various convection simulations. The associated code developed as part of this research is openly accessible and has been successfully integrated into the most recent version of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). The model has been incorporated into the Los Alamos National Laboratories research portfolio and is being considered for integration into the Energy Earth System Model, a next-generation global climate model developed by the Department of Energy as part of the ES-Perfomance model development programme. The model has also been submitted to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change for review as part of the Sixth Assessment Report. The proposed model has sparked a significant shift in thinking within the field of atmospheric convection research,

Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our findings demonstrate the intricate relationships between different types of entanglement in Jaynes-Cummings systems. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density. Further research aims to enhance the method's precision and extend it to other observables. This approach may provide a more objective method for identifying glueball states and could be adaptable to other contexts involving lattice field theory. This work is part of the LHCb efforts to enhance the understanding of lattice QCD through the use of experimental data from future experiments. This includes proposals for experiments that could see results as early as 2029. Another related study computes the lattice form factor for the two-body scattering process that creates a glueball from a meson pair, using the same method proposed here. This study aims to investigate the threshold behavior and possible signatures of threshold phenomena. Both studies contribute to the development of new methods for analyzing lattice QCD data, which can leverage the increasing availability of computationally intensive data, such as that generated by future flagships in lattice QCD. This will allow researchers to explore the complex structure of lattice spectra, revealing new insights into the fundamental theory of quantum chromodynamics. organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. An
interesting observation emerged when we adapted this model to analyze the sentiment ex-
pressed in subsequent tweets following a particular topic, represented by a specific central
tweet. We discovered that, to some extent, the model accurately reflected the evolution of
public sentiment in relation to the initial statement. In order to provide clarity to readers,
all code and data used in this project have been made freely available on GitHub. As a result,
new models and sentiment analysis datasets may be developed using this project's material.-

utilizing deep learning, in addition to presenting a novel application of this technology. We
also established a valuable resource that is beneficial to researchers working on similar projects.

learning models. 
Finally, we believe that our code and data can serve as a starting point for other projects 
involving sentiment analysis on Twitter.

or programming to design, train, and test a deep learning model.

tweets.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study demonstrates that the shadow radius can be an useful thermal entropy probe for understanding phase transition thermodynamics in black holes. Ultimately, we derive a formula for entropy based on shadow radius, which may be useful in resolving the entropy puzzle for black holes. Despite being a two-dimensional probe, the shadow radius is capable of uncovering first-order phase transition nature and could be instrumental in furthering our understanding of black hole physics. Lastly, we examine the connection between the shadow radius and entropy through a nonlinear monodromy problem. We find that the shadow radius is associated with the length of a semi-major axis in a projected tangent space, and both reflect the thermal profile behavior. Moreover, we find that entropy is linked to the area of a complete ellipse in this projected space, and both space aspects are related to each other via a nonlinear rotation. This rotation represents a non-linear version of the Euclidean Gibbons-Hawking ansatz. We anticipate that this shadow-based approach will contribute meaningfully to the study of black hole physics, especially in relation to the thermodynamics of these cosmic objects.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Additionally, we illustrate practical applications of this concept through examples involving multimode systems and suggesting that this approach can be extended to other continuous-variable systems. This research offers a new perspective on quantum tomography, revealing that important quantum properties can be inferred from limited information about an optical state rather than through a comprehensive reconstruction process.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and data generated by our approaches are made publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/role-constrained-oops.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results showed that certain insect growth regulators can reduce fungal pressure and increase yields and profit even without accounting for the limited number of observations. However, when considering the limited data, the rankings changed, and some treatments became more efficient. Furthermore, the disease pressure impact was significant across various quantile levels, leading to potential applications beyond agricultural disease management. We also demonstrated that our solution can be adapted to accommodate different distribution assumptions. To facilitate replication and further research, we made the R code and data available online. Ultimately, this approach provides a valuable tool for analyzing pesticide efficacy in low-replicate experiments.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, the proposed model's performance with n (n<4)
dimensions also surpasses the existing approaches, showcasing its effectiveness
on a larger scale. The proposed model's code is made publicly available for
use by the research community. The proposed approach to viewport prediction
has the potential to contribute to various applications like video compression,
streaming, and retargeting. The proposed model provides a novel solution for
the challenging problem of viewport prediction in 360-degree streaming videos.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Our proposed method provides a crucial enhancement to existing tensor network techniques. For further reading, please refer to the attached archive file. Moreover, additional details and numerical data are available in the attached text file. Additionally, a Python implementation is available online at the specified repository link. This work has been accepted for publication in Journal X.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided. This involves the discovery that certain potentials satisfy a unified inequality when combined with capacity in the L^p norm. Consequently, we have a more general inequality that may be specifically applicable to certain potential theories. In particular, this leads to improved anisotropic Minkowski type inequalities, providing a precise measure for the anisotropic Minkowski problem introduced in the reference provided. This refers to the determination of the most circumscribed convex body with given anisotropic mean curvature and volume, where specific anisotropic Minkowski type inequalities will provide a bound on the overhang when comparing two such convex bodies. Notably, this result holds significance in the study of minimal surfaces and partial differential equations. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. Unfortunately, this approach still leaves significant portions of relevant data unusable. This issue highlights the importance of developing strategies to handle such events, either by reducing the satellite's vulnerability to solar flares, identifying earlier indicators to prevent data from the onset of a glitch, or distinguishing glitches from other potential causes. Despite these challenges, the extremely low differences measured in the experiment demonstrate the viability of testing the weak equivalence principle in this context. Further work is necessary to enhance the detection method and minimize the impact of glitches in future, more sensitive experiments. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete. Specifically, we prove a graph G has a 2-strong shortest path cover if and only if it is 2-link forest-free, and provide an NP-hard polynomial-time approximation algorithm for this problem. We analyze the performance of this algorithm, showing it achieves a cover of size O(k^2 * log(n)) for any k-hops cover of the same graph. We note some interesting properties of specific graphs, including the fact that a complete graph only requires a 1-strong cover, while a star graph requires a 2-strong cover and has the highest ratio of required sets to number of vertices among all graphs without repeated edges. We also establish upper and lower bounds for the number of 2-strong covers for certain graphs, and determine the complexity of the minimum k-hops cover problem for forest graphs as W[1]-hard for any positive integer k. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Furthermore, in scenarios involving costly expert demonstrations, CoIL proves resilient. We also derive a theoretical cooperative Q-learning CoIL expression, showcasing the framework's connection to traditional reinforcement learning methods. The code for the proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework is available online.

Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. Conversely, we also found that users' intentional actions play a lesser role in the broad trend of increasing polarization. Instead, users are primarily responsive to existing online environments that steer them towards certain news sources. The implications of these findings are complex and multifaceted, and they raise important questions about the interconnected aspects of the Web and how they contribute to polarization in society. The detailed data sets available to us also present promising opportunities for conducting additional research into this topic. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. This analysis leverages a recent paper by Berstena and Oko, which demonstrated that the combined cyclic variant of three context-free languages can simulate any context-free language when considering complements. We also establish that the time complexity of solving V's word problem computationally is also no more than quadratically scaling with input size. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
This is evident because the system reaches a state where there is a constant current 
of phase-space flow in both directions, which is a key feature of a non-equilibrium 
steady state. Our research also highlights the importance of adjusting the 
discrete time parameter in relation to the system's natural time period in order 
to achieve maximum current.
Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that it is possible to observe two-way 
flow in a single photon system, which is an open system. This is noteworthy 
because many-open-systems, such as chemical reactions or laser systems, also 
exhibit two-way flow.
Our research also includes a theoretical analysis of a system in which the driving 
force varies continuously over time. This analysis indicates that a non-equilibrium 
steady state can only occur if there is a constant current in the system's phase 
space flow.
Finally, our study suggests that experimental evidence for non-equilibrium 
steady states can provide significant insights into the characteristics of driving 
forces and the surrounding environment. 
This knowledge can be used to design other open quantum systems that can achieve 
the same level of stability. 
In addition, our research paves the way for the extension of this study 
to systems that can be controlled continuously in time. 
This could involve the study of driving forces that have an irregular time base 
or the investigation of systems in which the time base of the driving force and 
the system's time base are linked in a complex manner. 
The study of such systems has the potential to give us a deeper understanding 
of how the time base of the driving force and the system's time base interact 
in open quantum systems.

Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Our work also establishes a connection between base p/q systems and the context-free language family, as well as providing an example showing that some context-free languages are recognisable in base p/q systems. Additionally, we are able to define a context-free expression that recognises all possible decimations of p/q. Our research provides both base p/q recognisability results and a context-free approach, offering a new perspective on base p/q systems that may also be applicable to other numbering systems. By defining a stronger system that includes additional symbols and operators, we are able to show that both base p/q systems and base p/q systems with natural order relation and modulo-p operator have the same recognisable sets when considering deterministic pushdown automata. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The resulting model is evaluated against a variety of observational limits including those from REST and X-ray observations, and the evaluation indicates that the model is compatible with these limits. The axion parameters are found to be somewhat constrained by the limits, and the sterile-neutrino parameters are found to be more heavily constrained by the limits, particularly those resulting from neutrino data. The model provides a possible framework for interpreting the cosmic microwave background and large scale structure observations, and it is also found to be compatible with the limits resulting from direct and indirect searches for DM. The interpretation of the data relies heavily on the flat tangent plane gauge within Higgs inflation, and thus it is possible that additional DM creation mechanisms may be required if an alternative gauge is used. The model also raises the possibility that the axion parameters may be heavily constrained by DM creation mechanisms, and thus it is possible that the existence of axions may be required by the data, independent of the strong CP problem. The analysis presented here lays the foundation for a more in-depth analysis of the model and its predictions, and it also raises a variety of theoretical and experimental questions that require additional investigation. The most pressing of these questions involves the interpretation of the data when an alternative gauge is used, and it also involves the possibility that the existence of axions may be required by the data, independent of the strong CP problem. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, we demonstrate real-world applications featuring the EG-CNN module in medical image processing. To facilitate further research, the source code for all experiments is openly available on GitHub. Overall, the Edge-Gated CNNs module offers a versatile, easily adaptable solution that can be seamlessly integrated into any CNN. It offers exceptional precision in edge extraction and has shown significant potential in complex medical image processing scenarios. The open-sourced code also enables other researchers to explore this concept across diverse image recognition contexts. The publicly accessible codebase can be found under the name 'Edge Gated Convolutional Neural Networks' on GitHub. The authors encourage contributions that help broaden the scope of this edge extraction module. The code can be found at the following address: https://github.com/sunscy/Edge-Gated-CNNs. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of MongoDB's transaction protocols, and discussed their implications on application development, including potential issues with phantom bugs. To facilitate future research on inter-operation with MongoDB transactions, we introduced a formal definition of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols, and validated that they meet specific requirements of weak consistency models. We also provided an analysis of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols in different deployment scenarios, and offered recommendations for application developers to avoid phantom bugs with MongoDB. Finally, we proposed an evaluation framework that can be used to assess the effectiveness of MongoDB's transaction protocols, and applied this framework to evaluate the correctness of MongoDB's transaction protocols in different deployment scenarios. We have publicly disclosed our findings in an easily accessible document, containing the pseudocode, formal definitions, and evaluation results for each MongoDB deployment scenario. Additionally, we have published a separate document that outlines the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols, including the weak consistency models they meet, and presented potential solutions to address the issue of phantom bugs with MongoDB. This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Furthermore, we establish a connection between the combinatorial proof and the approach employing the inverse of the inclusion matrix for Dyck paths in Cho-Huh (2019), revealing insights that can be applied to bounce numbers greater than three. As a result, we anticipate this technique to be a valuable tool for investigating the $e$-positivity of chromatic symmetric functions for higher bounce numbers.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the adverse impact of intrinsic bias on models when trained on biased datasets, even with the implementation of bias reduction techniques.  Our proposed framework is publicly accessible at https://github.com/yousefis/Bias-Quantification- Framework for Medical-Image-Analysis, and the code for our bias reduction experiments is available at https://github.com/yousefis/klotskinet.  Our study represents a pioneering effort to define a metric for intrinsic bias in medical image datasets and provides a comprehensive framework for identifying and quantifying biases, which is a critical consideration for developing reliable and generalizable medical image analysis models.  In the future, we plan to explore new techniques for reducing intrinsic bias and welcome collaborations and feedback from the research community.  In the future, we also aim to apply our proposed framework to other medical image segmentation tasks, such as mitosis segmentation from large datasets.  Additionally, we look to investigate new metrics for evaluating intrinsic bias and exploring new directions for bias reduction techniques.  Our work is a initial step towards addressing the critical issue of biases in medical image datasets and developing reliable and generalizable medical image analysis models. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. This finding implies that noise in similar complex networks might hold valuable informational content related to the system's assembly history. Lastly, the hysteresis loop shapes and noise patterns are influenced by the degree of fusion that defines the network's size and structure. This research is also backed by experimental data from the growth of a particular type of magnetic material, known as a ferrite, where the microstructure indeed consists of interconnected triangular structures. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. As a result, we developed a simplified model for predicting energy flux at various distances from the sun, with the aim of eventually using this type of modeling for a better understanding of how solar plasma structures form and behave. Despite its limitations, this model can still provide useful insights for planning missions intended to study solar wind structure and variability up close to the sun. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, our investigations lead to an overall understanding of how the material structure's symmetry implies the symmetry of limit functional norms. This research has been publicly shared to facilitate discussion and feedback.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. The generated models facilitate valuation of these systems and contribute to solving engineering challenges, inverse design issues, and potential educational and research pursuits. All our software models are available under a permissive license for public use at https://github.com/lclsii/cpa-nlo. We also invite users to contribute to our software through regular updates at https://github.com/lclsii/cpa-nlo/discussions.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. BART has been shown to be a viable model for this word ordering task and outperforms existing methods with a simple fine-tuning approach, with our code and data available at https://github.com/huggingface/distril language.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Furthermore, our technique showcases superior robustness and adaptability in low-data scenarios and outperforms existing methods with only 20 training examples per class. Our code has been made openly available on the GitHub platform. https://github.com/ghrzj/MD-CSDNetwork.git

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. However, we also observe that positive degree-degree correlations can result in performance degradation or even non-asymptotic suboptimality in tail error rates. In response to these discoveries, we devise optimized degree-degree correlated LDPC codes that can outperform their uncoded counterparts under various degree-degree correlation scenarios. Moreover, we highlight potential design guidelines for unequal error protection systems employing correlated LDPC codes. In doing so, we outline potential design strategies for both binary erasure channels and general communication channels, offering insights into the complex interplay between degree-degree correlations, channel conditions, and error patterns. Finally, we outline potential research paths for extending the scope of this work to multilevel correlations and non-binary settings. In doing so, we highlight the importance of developing numerical tools that can efficiently assess the performance of correlated LDPC codes across various channels and error patterns. In this research, we introduce one such solution, describing a newly developed program that can evaluate the performance of LDPC codes featuring multilevel degree-degree correlations over binary erasure channels, erasure multiplexing channels, and general communication channels, thereby providing a foundation for the generation of highly optimized correlated LDPC codes. A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Furthermore, with the source phase fixed, we found that the proposed attack can succeed in bypassing the system's security at an error rate indistinguishable from the real scenario, when the source phase is set to a specific value. Nevertheless, our proposed attack faces a limitation when dealing with the global phase of single photons, where its effectiveness depends on the specific system under attack. Given that the proposed attack can be executed with a simple photon source, without the need for quantum storage or manipulation of the multi-photon state, we believe this threat model poses a significant challenge to the global phase-encoding QKD baseline system. As such, we advise that measures be taken to mitigate this attack, such as rotating the source phase by a random degree or using phase-ramping techniques. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the critical importance of robust testing and secure establishment of communication in multi-user quantum networks. While applicable to baseline phase-encoding QKD, our findings may also have implications for other applications of quantum optics. Nonetheless, our proposed attack is expendable and can be defended against with minimal additional expense, leading us to conclude that its implementation would not significantly compromise the efficiency of these systems. Nonetheless, we believe our discovery warrants immediate attention from researchers actively developing phase-encoding QKD systems. Moreover, given the inherent simplicity of our proposed attack, we anticipate that it may be applicable to other applications of quantum optics. Ultimately, we contend that the communication networks in quantum computing systems require a secure foundation that goes beyond mere testing and protocol execution. As such, we urge a more fundamental approach to ensuring the integrity of these systems. As a starting point, we propose a new threshold test for quantum hacking, one that takes into account various hacking strategies and may serve as a benchmark for evaluating the security of quantum computing systems. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our methods on network scalability and interoperability with other networks, emphasizing the importance of standardization and robust testing for these techniques. Finally, we outline potential research paths for exploring other optimisation objectives in this network architecture. The proposed model is viable today, and we provide a reference implementation and data for interested parties to build upon. The underlying mathematical model and numerical results are also compatible with contemporary optimization tools. The work laid out here serves as a foundation for further research into the computational aspects of edge computing in multi-access networks. The associated code and data are available at https://git.io/gjK4J. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, it demonstrates the applicability of these solutions to certain distinct scenarios. Last but not least, it addresses a question that was related to these problems, which was posed by J. Hlavacek in 1931. This involves the topic of spaces with angle functions that have a specific order and are characterized by the property of betweenness. The article offers an alternative proof for Hlavacek's theorem and also explores additional consequences that result from the defined angle function being order-preserving. All the proofs provided in this article rely solely on the basic properties of the space with angle function, which it argues, should be considered the fundamental framework. Hence, the article suggests that this structure deserves closer attention in the context of geometry. Lastly, the article introduces new problems related to these concepts, which it hopes will stimulate further research in this field. This article is a revised version of the author's 2015 thesis, which was submitted to the Faculty of Physical Mathematics at the Palacky University in Olomouc. It has undergone extensive modification to improve its clarity and is now presented in a more user-friendly format. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Additionally, we present non-trivial examples of bounds for specific ratios of minima in quadratic, cubic, and quartic number fields. Moreover, we describe a method for counting the number of embeddings of a degree $n$ number field into the complex plane up to conjugation, using minima to express this count as an integer valued function of lengths in the field. Lastly, we offer an approach to classify the geometry of inequalities solely based on field properties, offering a starting point to address Lenstra's conjecture. 

This work is inspired by several sources, including recent research on the geometry of inequalities within number fields and fields of transcendental numbers, as well as the ongoing discussion on Lenstra's conjecture. It represents an initial foray into the study of the geometry of inequalities in number fields, offering a perspective on the relationships between minima and the structure of number fields, and providing a foundation for further exploration into the interplay between these geometric considerations and arithmetic properties of fields and their automorphism groups. 

This paper is an extension of prior work presented at conferences, where parts of the research were discussed in conference talks, and feedback from attendees helped refine the research directions.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for determining pressure. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment over a pressure range (1-1.5 bar), the method effectively captures intricate pressure variations resulting from nitrous gas interacting with a solid surface in various states of flow. Notably, it can also detect very fine-scale pressure differences arising from the conversion of kinetic energy into pressure as well as distinct O2/N2 patterns formed by turbulent mixing processes. Visualizations reveal rich information about coherent vortices, turbulent oscillations, and irregular movements within these systems. Throughout a 10-minute observation period, the technique maintains high sensitivity, resolving down to 50 ms for pressure and 110 ms for oxygen concentration. In addition to its applications to studying flow dynamics and gas-phase diagnostics, this technique may also find value in monitoring respiratory therapy. By offering simultaneous measurements of multiple parameters with high resolution and accuracy, it provides a powerful tool for a broad range of research and medical monitoring scenarios. In its current form, the technique has a relatively narrow observation window but future developments could expand this capability. In a system as complex as the human brain, researchers often rely on recording electrical activity through EEG. Similarly, in respiratory systems, monitoring gas-phase conditions could aid in understanding airflow dynamics and facilitate improvements to respiratory design by identifying areas of high shear stress, lung regions that need further development, and optimizing oxygen supply by minimizing concentration variations. In a simple model consisting of two connected cylinders, pressure drops significantly (up to 2 bar) in a matter of seconds when the gas is pumped out of one chamber.
