The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation. This model offers a possible solution to the planetary system "great gap problem" and could provide a connection between planetary formation and the disappearance of protoplanetary disks. Further research is needed to fully understand this process and its implications for planetary formation. This study provides a comprehensive exploration of this model's principles and suggests several ways it could be refined or expanded upon. Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that backscattering between opposing modes at the contact locations is present. The result shows that neutral modes hold relevant information and can be used for a nonlocal reconstruction of a dc charge current. The described protocol may be employed to detect any neutral mode that counter-propagates with respect to charge modes, and this detection approach is applicable not only to the edge modes of quantum Hall systems but also to systems possessing neutral modes that do not originate from quantum Hall effects. Finally, an experimental demonstration of this concept is proposed. The relationship between this neutral mode detection phenomenon and the quantum eddy current anomaly is discussed. The quantity measured in this anomaly is reinterpreted as a neutral mode counter-propagating with respect to charge modes in the quantum eddy current anomaly, and neutral mode counter-propagating behavior is predicted for the quantum eddy current anomaly in a certain material configuration. The investigation of this neutral mode counter-propagating behavior is proposed as an experimental protocol on a case-by-case basis for different materials experiencing the quantum eddy current anomaly. The quantum eddy current anomaly refers to an anomalous Hall eddy current that exhibits a quantum effect when the magnetic field is strong. The quantum eddy current anomaly is distinct from the regular eddy current which is caused by the absorption of photons by electrons and results in a heat transfer, in contrast to the quantum eddy current anomaly which is a quantum effect resulting in a charge current instead. We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Consequently, the basis \bar{Θ} provides a significant improvement to existing constructions of quantum group bases, such as Lusztig's, Darboux's, and Haouzi's. Additionally, our rigidity condition yields an explicit classification of the quantum group U_q(g), leading to new possibilities for applying its subalgebra structure in the study of quantum cluster algebras. For type ADE, we establish a natural projection from the quantum group U_q(g) to the braid group U_g(B_g), extending the classical case proposed by Lusztig in 2000. We also develop an explicit 'quantization' of the classical Weyl group invariants C(WG ∘), leading to an explicit classification of U_q(g) through its action on the quantum cluster variety O_q(P_G ∘). This quantization can be viewed as an extension of Haouzi's 'deformed' basis construction from 2016, allowing us to exploit the quantum duality of cluster algebras to achieve a more direct derivation of the quantum group structure. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Our research extends the application of DRO models in real-world scenarios with significant data sets. DR-DSGD is implemented as an open-source PyTorch framework on GitHub. This new approach makes an important contribution to the field, addressing the challenge of data shift in decentralized learning networks. The code is available at: https://github.com/yousefian/DR-DSGD. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. Moreover, we make publicly accessible, in an open-source database, both pressure data and different variations of the used simulation methods and pressure estimation algorithms. This initiative is intended to promote collaboration and contribute to establishing common standards for evaluating the validity of physical interpretations of the hard-disk model by comparing them with the documented results. This initiative is part of an open-letter campaign that aims to launch a scientific debate within the computational physics community. The debate should address fundamental questions regarding the design of ideal equilibrium tests, the reliability of different simulation methods, the validity of their application to model systems that do not reach equilibrium, and the practical usefulness of simultaneously running multiple independent simulations. The debate is crucial for addressing the hard-disk model's critical issues, such as understanding the phase-transition scenario, predicting the exact temperature at which the transition occurs, determining whether there is a distinct transition point, and what factors influence the transition by affecting how disks interact with each other. The debate should involve experts in the field, young researchers, and anyone interested in contributing to the discussion by sharing their results, opinions, or both. The initial set of results presented in this paper has been achieved by collaborating with F. Calatroni, who used a simulation method that leveraged many computer processors simultaneously and provided pressure data that were subsequently analyzed by us using different pressure estimation algorithms. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored. Our findings indicate that jet modification simulations depend considerably on nuclear PDF and medium parameters, and suggest that JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4 overestimate the extent of jet outreach into the medium. Adjusting the medium's temperature to match the energy loss model ELISA within JEWEL brings the outlook of jets into alignment with experimental data. The study highlights the necessity for a unified understanding of jet interaction with the nuclear medium and available nuclear PDF sets, and stresses the significance of developing better experimental constraints on jet modification in nuclear collisions. Furthermore, it is proposed that distinct jet PDFs be developed to incorporate nuclear modification effects. Finally, in addition to nuclear PDFs, the scale choice associated with the medium's temperature also requires differentiation to accurately describe various medium conditions, particularly in scenarios where the medium's temperature is low and the energy density is high. The study suggests that energy loss models could be refined to directly relate to the choice of scale, and urges the development of better experimental access to medium conditions, such as open charm or heavy-flavor photodisintegration, to dissect nuclear PDFs and understand jet modification in nuclear collisions. The findings from this study can be utilized to interpret future data, and provide a foundation for theoretical model improvements. They also emphasize the necessity for simultaneous evolution of perturbative jet and nuclear PDFs to accurately model jet modification in nuclear collisions. Ultimately, this study aims to stimulate the development of better experimental and theoretical understanding of jet modification within nuclear medium, and encourages the exploration of new perspectives on this complex topic. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. With revenues exceeding $200 million in daily transactions and 20,000 daily new users at the scheme's peak in April 2021, Forsage has been notable for attracting a substantial number of users from low-income countries. In conclusion, Forsage represents a unique opportunity to study pyramid schemes in action and shows how easily these fraudulent operations can be executed with minimal expenses, thanks to the ease of creating and executing blockchain smart contracts. Furthermore, our research indicates that Forsage's success can be attributed to the appeal of cryptocurrency investment, coupled with the anonymity of the internet, rather than any inherent characteristics of blockchain technology. In addition, our study reveals that Forsage's structure allows it to evade detection by most cryptocurrency anti-money laundering systems. With Forsage shut down in July 2021 following legal action from the SEC, we believe our research offers timely insights into the workings and implications of this high-profile pyramid scheme. In addition, our methods for analyzing Forsage could be applied to any blockchain-based multi-level marketing platforms. We also propose several potential measures to differentiate legitimate multi-level marketing companies from pyramid schemes and include a discussion on the challenges and potential solutions for detecting these schemes within cryptocurrency transaction networks. We conclude that while blockchain-based pyramid schemes pose a challenging problem for detection due to the visibility of transactions, they also present a unique opportunity for in-depth examination of these fraudulent operations. We hope our research will inspire further investigation into the intricate workings of these schemes and the effectiveness of our methods in analyzing them. We have made our custom-made transaction simulator and other methods for analyzing Forsage available on GitHub.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We based our determinations on RR Lyrae star counts within the proposed cluster regions, estimating a range from 2 to 15 thousand stars based on RR Lyrae quantities, predicting the smallest four candidates would contain less than 10 thousand stars while the largest four would have between 12 and 15 thousand stars. A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. Our study provides detailed NNLL$'$-resummation order analysis (combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions) to fully comprehend the primary and secondary quark-mass influences for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all pertinent scale relationships. Notably, in case of the $q_T$ distribution, distinct rapidity divergences arise, leading to an intricate understanding of rapidity evolution features, paving the way for precise quark-mass measurements at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. Conversely, in $Z$-gap jet function, our research anticipates a significant role of LHC in exploring quark-mass effects thoroughly, offering a complementary perspective to those derived from global analyses of bottom-quark distribution in top-quark decay in a ratio of $t$-channel vector boson production to deep inelastic scattering, where a detailed investigation of the primary contributions of heavy-quark pairs splitting into gluons across various scale relationships is anticipated. Ultimately, our study provides a framework for a thorough understanding of quark-mass dependencies in exclusive differential distributions, empowering precise measurements and potential deviations from STU anomalous dimensions in a data-driven manner. As a result, this study is expected to contribute significantly to the comprehensive analysis of quark-mass effects in global fits of parton distribution functions, particularly in evaluating the primary contributions of heavy-quark pairs splitting into gluons

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We anticipate that this correction will be useful for other applications of tight-binding models. To facilitate experimental interpretation, we present a formulation of the optical sum rules for finite systems. We also investigate the influence of measurement time on optical properties, introducing the concept of the static correlation length to relate this effect to materials architecture. The proposed methods have been made publicly accessible through their incorporation into the ESPresO Python package. We anticipate that the precise simulation of optical properties in relation to gauge invariance will become a crucial tool for the design of materials with exceptional light-matter interaction properties. We look forward to contributing to the ongoing discussion of light-matter interaction simulations through the inclusion of additional models and theories. We invite the research community to participate in this discussion by contributing to the ESPresO package.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Furthermore, our findings pave the way for further
research into the behavior of deep learning models in relation to process dynamics. 

This study uniquely contributes in the following ways: 
- It's the first time Graph Neural Networks have been tested for process prediction
- It assesses deep learning models in different process stages that are determined
  objectively by event quantities and case completion times
- It reveals surprising outcomes where the basic Multi-layer Perceptron frequently
  outperforms more advanced models
- It shows that due consideration must be given to baselines like simple
  Multi-layer Perceptron along with the behavior of deep learning models in relation
  to process dynamics. 

In order to facilitate reproducibility, the code and data used for this research
is readily available for retrieval. 

Finally, this study extends the scope of deep learning applications in process
mining and provides valuable insights for both practitioners and researchers. These
insights can aid in the advancement of research into enhancing the predictiveness
of process models. 

In addition, this study employs the influential ProGEN+ dataset, a well-respected
benchmark, in order to ensure the reliability of its findings. 

Ultimately, this research uniquely contributes to the direction for further
investigation into how deep learning models behave under different process conditions. 
In order to advance the field, we recommend testing advanced deep learning models
against strong baselines in process-mining contexts.

Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This finding suggests that this two-component electron beam model can be applied to white-light flares on smaller stars, such as AU Mic, where star spots and flare activity are being closely monitored, including a notable superflare that occurred in 2011. We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult to model the network's behavior over extended periods of time. However, it has been proven possible to transform the network into an equivalent bipartite network with double the variables, allowing for analysis of systems that interact with themselves using traditional methods. This breakthrough enables a deeper examination of how systems behave during transitional and extended periods of time. Lastly, we investigate networks that interact with multiple components and are utilized in gene regulation systems by transforming these systems into equivalent bipartite networks that interact through pairs of elements. It is shown that these types of systems, where the flow of information is bidirectional, have the capacity to develop multiple equilibrium states, a key requirement for systems that manage life across various cell types. Moreover, we demonstrate that systems with fully connected subgraphs can showcase polynomial convergence to equilibrium, whereas systems with partially connected subgraphs converge according to a power law. Lastly, we highlight the significance of these findings by comparing them to similar systems that operate under different rules and mechanisms. We also present a detailed analysis of a real-world biological network that interacts with itself and is involved in gene regulation systems, used for cell-type specification. We propose that the unique properties of these types of systems could help us understand the intricate mechanisms behind life's complexity. Lastly, we hypothesize that a similar analysis could be applied to other interactive systems that operate according to Boolean rules and manage complex processes in living organisms. We conclude by presenting possible directions for further research in this field. We have written a Python module called NetDynamics that enables users to model and study systems that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, and we have attached this module to our study as a useful tool for researchers in this field. We believe that this module can be a valuable asset for users seeking to model and analyze systems that interact with themselves, and we hope that it may inspire further innovation in this field. We look forward to contributing to this field through ongoing research and development of NetDynamics. We have made NetDynamics available online at https://github.com/AlbertoBerm

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems. Additionally, we incorporate their utilization into our existing iterative method for obtaining self-consistent HFB solutions, and find this to be an efficient approach for obtaining accurate and symmetric HFB configurations even in heavily deformed nuclei. As an example, we calculate energy spectra and probability distributions for states like prolate and oblate deformations, specific quasiparticle configurations, and systems like $^{240}$Pu and $^{232}$Th. Our results obtained using these formulae are consistent with previously published data. This method will be an valuable tool for our on-going studies of collective phenomena in heavy radial nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing. Lastly, we include two practical applications showcasing how TPC can be applied to enhance the security of neural network-based point cloud models in vehicle navigation and object detection scenarios. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. The
code for our research is available at https://github.com/hubofhub/Time-LowFER.

Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Moreover, studies have further found that the majority of these complex poles lie below the threshold of the $\alpha$-particle decay and, what's more, that they are closely related to $\alpha$-particle scattering resonances within the same system, thus providing a new perspective on the topic. This breakthrough research highlights the significance of exploring many-body systems using a full spectral function, in particular by locating and interpreting complex excited states that contribute to broad resonances. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. In all cases, our algorithm showcases excellent performance in comparison to random walk-based methods, as evidenced by lower mean squared errors and better visualization of clustered data. Additionally, this approach is complementary to model-based analysis, providing practical insights that can inform and be validated by dynamical systems models. The authors also explore the method's scalability by employing GPU acceleration to achieve significant speed gains without compromising clustering accuracy. The code for this work has been made publicly accessible on GitHub, along with additional resources that are part of the paper's supplementary material. Furthermore, results from the Amazon rainforest and the 39-bus transmission network are presented in the form of video visualizations, showcasing the clustering of European collid dynamic maps and nonlinear load dynamics, respectively. The algorithms used in this work have been open-sourced on GitHub, along with the data used in the Amazon rainforest and the 39-bus transmission network, along with the embedded visualization tools that were employed to create the interactive visualizations presented in the paper. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. The vacuum stability criteria serves as a guideline for the structure of these energy levels, with the consequence that there must exist at least two of them. The model further suggests that dark matter might be connected to the largest energy level, which could be verified through direct detection experiments in combination with a parton shower analysis. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. Additionally, we have made the data and code associated with our research publicly available, in the hope that it will contribute to advancements in the analysis of broadcast location data, and facilitate a more detailed understanding of the complex dynamics of football matches. This approach can serve as a foundation for more comprehensive valuing of football teams' offensive strategies, and we have tabulated the predicted probabilities of ball gain and being attacked for all teams that competed in the 2020 European Football Championship. This research has also introduced a novel way to account for the diversity of players, based on their individual location data, and we have provided insights into the performance of defender teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, using the overlapping location of all players involved in game events. This has enabled us to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex, based on the overlapping location of all players involved in game events, and we have introduced a method for adjusting the predictions according to the diversity of players, based on the distribution of their location. We have used this approach to analyze the diversity of players in all teams that competed in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our results show that our approach can provide a more detailed understanding of the complex dynamics of football

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we provide a suite of artificial networks suitable for testing and validating measurement methods in various scenarios. The full study, including the normed methods and benchmark datasets, is accessible online. Implementing these normalized methods to notable datasets, such as Congress elections and Twitter users, revealed notable findings on the polarization levels in these societies. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. As such, we can examine the behavioral transitions of multilayer networks and the effects of interlayer connections on oscillators' synchronization. By leveraging our joint matrix representation, we can further explore its applicability to other multilayer systems and associated problems. Unlike conventional approaches for individual layers, our method provides a more integrated perspective on multilayer networks, offering a more coherent view of the system that goes beyond the analysis of individual components. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. Additionally, this work offers an interesting view on the Einstein operator's properties, including its role in the symmetrized tensor format, the relationship between its components and those of the Bianchi operator, and the connection between its divergence and the Einstein operator itself. This work also explores interesting properties of the Einstein operator's eigenvalues and eigen tensors, discussing both general theoretical considerations and specific eigen tensors derived from geometric configurations. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena. Furthermore, it paves the way for applying symmetry protection principles to other phenomena, such as momentum conservation, in this regime. Moreover, this study demonstrates the capability of cavity QED systems to exhibit symmetry-protected multi-quanta phenomena and facilitates the development of more complex quantum phases and collections of atoms trapped inside cavity arrays. This involves the case of trimer molecules, whose entangled states could be insulated against decay when combined with extremely strong coupling. This research also illustrates the capability of cavity QED to offer powerful means to create a variety of multi-quanta phenomena protected by symmetry, specifically in trimer systems. This is achieved by manipulating flip rates and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction to preserve parity. This work anticipates the necessity of a computational theory of multi-quanta emission that goes beyond single-system considerations and anticipates the possibility of multi-quanta emission in cavity QED being vastly more intricate than expected. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. These characteristics make the algorithm versatile and effective across a wide spectrum of applications, including the distribution of degrees in sparse complex networks and the estimation of network size in scenarios of uncertainty. We introduce a new probabilistic protocol called the "Degree Finder" that facilitates the identification of approximate degree holdings among fellow network nodes, either authentic or untrusted, by enabling the exchange of degree information between randomly selected node pairs. We prove the efficacy of this protocol in predicting the distribution of degrees among network nodes. We also examine various scenarios, including networks with diverse degree distributions and power-law characteristics, based on synthetic and real-world data. Moreover, we apply this protocol to estimate the distribution of distances between pairs of nodes, referred to as the "degree distance distribution," which differs significantly from the actual distance distribution. We validate our findings through simulations and comparisons with actual data for several complex networks, in addition to analyzing the overhead and accuracy of the algorithm across various scenarios. Notably, the Davis-Paxson model class, which includes fully connected and binary tree networks, can be exploited by malicious nodes to completely undermine the algorithm. In contrast, our analysis demonstrates that the algorithm succeeds even when confronted with an unbounded number of malicious nodes representing an arbitrarily small fraction of the total network size. We emphasize the importance of distinguishing between actual and predicted degree distributions to ensure effectiveness. queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

using the proposed method and two traditional methods, neutron and green wave, 
for 30,679 observations, also incorporating different CO (degree of capacity 
occupation) levels. The study's results in terms of mean squared error (MSE) show 
that the proposed method yields similar accuracy when compared to the two other 
methods; also discussed are limitations of the current approach and potential 
paths for future research. The study's findings and methods are available online

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. This breakthrough provides a substantial performance enhancement, enabling the computation of conformally flat spacetimes with 10-20 resolutions within a single day on a single computer processor. However, it also reveals that the success of this method relies heavily on the resolution of the spacetime grid, where further research is needed to expand its applicability to higher resolutions. This new approach has the potential to drive major breakthroughs in prominent scenarios, such as spacetimes surrounded by scalar clouds. This, in turn, may lead to a deeper understanding of the issues associated with solving the Hamiltonian constraint in nonlinear theories of gravity. This work is a critical contribution to the current efforts of the Numerical Relativity Community, given the fundamental importance of solving the Hamiltonian constraint in generating initial data for gravitational physics. This study is a crucial step in preparing large-scale parameter studies required to analyze the behavior of unstable black hole solutions in fundamental field theories. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate notable enhancements in the anomalous Nernst effect and conductivity when considering the thermal gradient effect, resulting in a primary contribution of this study. Notably, our results yield a primary contribution of this study, where the anomalous Nernst effect shows substantial enhancements in antiferromagnetic Mn$_3$NiN thin films when the thermal gradient is considered. Moreover, this study provides a foundation for a comparative analysis of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects in antiferromagnetic materials. Further, our research indicates that the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials can be anticipated using the scattering factor and conductivity measured during the same experiment, enabling a theoretical prediction of the anomalous Nernst coefficient from the measured anomalous Hall coefficient and conductivity. By validating our model using the measured data of the current study and existing literature, our theoretical framework offers a valuable tool for predicting the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials with unique electronic structures and magnetic properties. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As demonstrated with data across multiple user projects, this approach facilitates real-time data analysis to produce actionable results during the experiment, reducing data analysis times to near real-time. This work highlights several machine learning models, covering topics like crystallographic phase identification, orientation determination, strain measurement, and chemical composition analysis. By integrating these models with user projects, we showcase significant improvements to data quality, accuracy, and precision, achieving results that would be difficult or time-consuming to obtain through traditional analysis. To facilitate replication and advancement of this work, all code and models are openly available on GitHub. By integrating machine learning into user facilities through this framework, we aim to empower a greater range of researchers to leverage this technology and enhance the machine learning landscape as a community. This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. Additionally, a specific value for the anomalous heat cross-flux can be derived from the linear results, demonstrating a connection to the anisotropy-induced mode frequency growth. A linear stability analysis and mode frequency growth are calculated in a current tokamak device, with results showing that even small ion temperature anisotropy can significantly affect GAM stability. A numerical tool is implemented to efficiently solve the complex problem of nonlinear GAM spectrum in future tokamaks on the road to the development of a burning fusion plasma. Leveraging this development, the potential for the ITER tokamak to achieve breakeven performance is assessed, with results indicating that achieving a stable GAM frequency around 1 kHz could serve as an indicator of stable core plasma conditions during ITER operations. Furthermore, this study proposes that monitoring GAMs in ITER via electromagnetic flux measurements may provide valuable insights into understanding core plasma stability and sharing data with other experimental devices. With the aim of making such measurements feasible, recommendations are made to incorporate specialized sensors capable of detecting GAMs in future tokamaks, as well as to adopt an integrated approach to data analysis that takes into account the interactions between different plasma microturbulences and their possible links with wall-protected plasma regions. This integrated approach is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of plasma stability that takes into account the interactions between the core and boundary plasmas in future devices leading to the development of a burning fusion plasma. This development is expected to pave the way for successful implementation of innovative magnetic configurations with improved confinement and significantly higher fusion gains in large tokamaks. This development is crucial for the success of fusion devices and will provide a solid foundation for a potential future expansion to other fusion devices, such as stellarators and burning plasma devices. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Moreover, our research offers a potential solution to tackle Hamiltonians featuring non-stoquastic interactions, a significant barrier in the field. The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. As such, it addresses the need for a more empirical approach to developing evidence-based online learning design principles in higher education. In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. 
Ultimately, our findings underscore the capability and versatility of the paracomplete
and paraconsistent logic system within a realistic theoretical framework. We conclude
by outlining potential avenues for further exploration in this context.

BZFC-system, Tarski semantics, satisfaction relation.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of using a non-invasive BCI approach with high resolution recordings to control the most complex aspect of gait, suggesting a bright future for the development of more sophisticated lower limb prosthetics powered by the brain.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Alongside outstanding performance, DECENNT-generated graphs provide actionable insights for researchers and experts in various domains. The code for DECENNT is now available on GitHub.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. The evaluation is conducted across a range of tree and network topologies, alongside assessments of network density, size, and the frequency of specific reticulate patterns. A finding emerges that suggests a distinction should be drawn between "true" network generators and those that merely transpose trees into network form, the latter including the former as a special case. Furthermore, our research entails a novel extension of the Downton distribution to models of phylogenetic network size, enabling predictive modeling of network characteristics. Alongside these comparisons, recommendations for future research and development in phylogenetic network generation are put forth. Ultimately, our study aims to foster enhanced understanding and more informed decision making in the development and application of phylogenetic network generators. In doing so, we make available a suite of interactive visualization tools to facilitate comparison among these tools. Alongside the comparison results for each dataset, the study is accompanied by a suite of network examples, alongside the source code for the network generators and visualization tools used in the research. The code is hosted on GitHub at the address mentioned in the study. The research is concurrent with the EU-ALGCO 2020 conference and the extended version of the study is published in the Journal of Mathematical Biology. The journal article is accompanied by an interactive visualization showcasing the comparison results for different network generators. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed algorithm has significant potential to contribute to various biological and technological applications such as analyzing animal locomotion, studying biologically inspired robotics, detecting health issues from gait patterns in medical biometrics, identifying potential threats from security biometrics, and enhancing video surveillance. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The study will be valuable in pinpointing the MSSM Higgs sector, given the forthcoming precision measurements, specifically the dominant contributions in the complex parameter scenario. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. The methodology is applied to real-world data sets, incorporating healthcare treatment outcomes and network stock return data. Implemented methods are made publicly available through the R package 'NetAR.R'.

However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. The proposed efficient algorithms for robust vector pooling and optimal transport provide valuable insights into optimizing the interaction between forward and backward passes across diverse declarative networks. The experimental evaluations of these algorithms highlight substantial gains in computational efficiency, along with precise control over robustness, and demonstrate their integration into comprehensive neural networks. The explicit manipulation of optimization dynamics through computational graphics techniques opens up fresh avenues for innovative design in declarative networks. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed approach methods established 'active fluid mechanics' models which treat cells as two-dimensional fluid surfaces with temporarily fixed patterns of contractility. Our model distinguishes between and refines the behavior of single proteins and actin networks, incorporating the reorganization of actin filaments into a reaction-diffusion process that influences cellular spreading and movement. This framework has practical application in simulating and better understanding the relationship between protein membrane properties and cellular spreading, as observed in recent experiments. We validate our method by reading and analyzing existing 'active fluid mechanics' models, incorporating their assumptions and limitations into our multi-faceted framework. This new approach now allows for the simulation of a cell's spreading and movement at various scales, encompassing the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. We utilize this framework to explore the impact of external forces on cytoskeletal network behavior and the influence of network structure on protein membrane properties through a process of parameter exploration. We have developed a computer program that executes this multi-faceted approach and is readily available for public use. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By uncovering cyclic patterns within transaction graphs, our method is anticipated to enhance the detection efficiency of existing anti-money laundering techniques by identifying related transactions that were previously disconnected. Furthermore, our approach is capable of providing more comprehensive and accurate insights into money trails and cryptocurrency transaction analysis. As a demonstration of its efficacy, our study presents the detection of two unknown malicious projects conducted over several months. The research presented is supported by an open-source software available for other blockchain platforms at our GitHub repository. The study has been reviewed by multiple cryptocurrency experts with a blockchain background of over 100 years combined. The research is also accompanied by a comprehensive evaluation based on expert feedback from the blockchain community. The study is further characterized by the inclusion of multiple malicious projects identified through the proposed approach, in addition to the analysis of two specific temporal cyclic transfers.
