Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our decoder framework facilitates natural integration with decoding improvements, such as the incorporation of external data or new decoding techniques, by constructing decoders as state transitions that can be tailored through reward functions. Ultimately, our approach enables the development of robust, adaptable decoders that can efficiently handle complex quantum error scenarios. This innovative framework also provides a versatile platform for exploring novel decoding concepts and enriching our understanding of deepQ learning applications in quantum computation. By unleashing the potential of deepQ learning in this domain, we anticipate a surge in the development of innovative solutions, along with the ability to tackle intricate scenarios that were previously difficult to manage. As such, this approach is expected to contribute significanly to the advancement of surface code research and the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing. As a testament to this, we have already implemented several decoders utilizing this approach and made them publicly available for the benefit of the quantum computing community. This includes a decoder capable of handling biased readout errors, as well as one capable of integrating measurement bias and noise duration as separate factors. Furthermore, we have introduced the concept of incorporating physical properties of quantum systems when deploying near-term quantum error correction, utilizing a case study of a quantum simulator. By leveraging the capabilities of this framework, we believe it to be an ideal foundation for exploring novel decoding concepts and developing practical decoders that can be applied to real-world quantum systems. As such, we encourage the community to contribute their innovative decoding solutions, as well as share their own experiences in this space. All of our code has been made publicly available at the specified repository. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. To validate the simulation-based findings, a physical one-legged hopping robot was built and tested. While the physical robot exhibited similar performance in response to the feedback controller, it failed to match the simulation's efficiency in reaching the desired height. Nonetheless, the feedback controller proved effective in reducing height errors even with a much smaller foot size (15cm^2) in real-world experiments. This work's feedback control system and DEM simulation-based model can be applied to more complex multipedal robots operating on deformable terrain. Additionally, it provides a method for evaluating the impact of gear ratios and foot forces on the effectiveness of the feedback controller in such environments. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. Furthermore, the droplet's oscillatory behavior could be tailored to modify the surrounding air's properties, thus potentially enriching the physics involved and facilitating the transport of heat and mass. The oscillatory droplet presents a unique opportunity for investigating the interplay between chemical reactions, diffusion, and convection in this two-phase system, with implications for various applications, including combustion processes, environmental topics, and chemical processes, the latter involving droplets serving as receptors for chemical agents. The droplet's ability to modulate the circulation of the surrounding air also presents a chance to optimize the mass transfer process by selecting the most suitable electron energy in the resonating electric field, thus potentially enhancing the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity. The present study introduces a novel numerical approach that combines the implementation of the Navier-Stokes equations and the droplet's oscillatory behavior, allowing for the creation of an aerosol cloud and the simulation of the droplet's interaction with the surrounding air and particulate matter. The proposed method is applied to investigate the effect of an electrical field on a droplet in the presence of an aerosol cloud and reveals that the droplet's oscillatory behavior, induced by the electrical field, results in the generation of vortices that impede the attraction of particulate matter, while also stabilizing the aerosol cloud and hindering the transport of air between droplets. Additionally, the simulation demonstrates that the droplet's ability to modify the circulation of the surrounding air facilitates the optimization of the mass transfer process. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. As we look toward the future, we hope CONDAQA will serve as a catalyst for the development of more sophisticated models capable of accurately processing negation within NLP community. Additionally, we developed a visualization tool to present the inferred topic structures and enable users to explore and navigate the network based on the identified topics. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The associated quantum quench dynamics span multiple degrees of freedom and involve intricate correlations between those degrees of freedom. The statistical analysis employed here involves the conventional evaluation of annealing gap estimates, as well as the training of neural networks, the latter occurring through the application of backpropagation and related optimization techniques. The underlying Hamiltonian models include arbitrary single-body and randomly generated two-body interaction terms, thereby encompassing a vast spectrum of quench and annealing dynamics. The empirical results indicate that the behavior of annealing gap can be accurately replicated through the training of compact neural networks containing a mere 10-50 trainable parameters, a remarkable finding given the intricate nature of the associated quantum quench dynamics. The success of this approach suggests that the development of optimized quantum annealing protocols can be achieved through the training of similar-scale neural networks, a prospect that may provide a meaningful solution to the challenges posed by the development of large-scale quantum annealing. A possible future direction in this area could involve the extension of this study to other types of Hamiltonians and Hamiltonian models that incorporate time-dependent parameters, a scenario that would require a separate development of neural network training algorithms capable of handling such scenarios. Ultimately, this study indicates that the complexity of quantum annealing can be grasped through the understanding of quantum quench dynamics, a perspective that may lead to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships governing the quench and annealing dynamics, as well

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. It also presents novel approaches to conformance checking that can handle partial process runs and offers technicians more flexible options to accommodate varying real-world scenarios. These new methods are evaluated with process data from the healthcare industry, using reference models to compare observed process patterns with recommended best practices. Results from these evaluations are presented and assess the methods' effectiveness in comparing full and partial process runs. Furthermore, they highlight differences in analysis outcomes between full and partial process runs and provide insights into the methods' potential applications in real-world settings. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential for alignments to support the development and evaluation of highly effective reference models within process improvement initiatives. It also lays the groundwork for future research to expand the technique's healthcare-specific aspects and ensure its broader usability across various processes. Finally, due to the recent developments in conformance checking, related research is now feasible, and this study is a first step towards that research. It is accompanied by an open-source tool that enables alignments to be performed on full or partial process runs and is available under the name of Conformance Checker (Confe) on GitHub. The source code for the techniques discussed in the study is available on GitHub under the name Confe (Conformance Checker). The findings from the evaluation are presented and assess the techniques' effectiveness when analyzing both full and partial process runs. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Includes discussions on both the limitations of such one-band approximations and
possible experimental avenues for validation. 
Also includes an exploration of possible phase diagrams as materials are
changed from idealized models.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Lastly, the results are validated through direct numerical simulations.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Concurrent testing
also enables continuous integration and continuous deployment methods. Experimental
results using an open source database demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. We also explore possible applications to other software systems. The implementation is available online. Keywords: software maintenance; regression testing; singular value decomposition; parallel calculation; continuous integration and continuous deployment. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Our research employed Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, and Logistic Regression algorithms to analyze the context of the dataset, with the latter demonstrating the highest accuracy. Furthermore, the paper examines context learning from the dataset, showcasing the complexity of big data through a simple yet effective approach. Our research incorporates a comprehensive overview of feature extraction methods, emphasizing the advantages of context learning. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we incorporated an example related to sentiment context. The primary contribution of this paper is the context learning of big data through a simple approach, showcasing the complexity of big data through an example and highlighting the significance of context learning. The paper also emphasizes the importance of sentiment analysis in daily life, presenting novel perspectives on interpreting the context of big data. The context learning results presented in the paper provide new insights that can be utilized in various applications, paving the way for further research and analysis. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. We then demonstrate that this restriction is NP-hard by showing a reduction from the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem. We also discuss the limitations of our algorithm and the properties of anti Tai mapping by examining its relationship with the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem. We conclude that studying anti Tai mapping as a binary relationship between trees enriches our understanding of the concept of Tai mapping and its associated algorithms. We present our results as a form of future research relevant to the field. We then suggest potential directions for further investigation, including the extension of anti Tai mapping to ordered trees and the examination of maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. We also propose adding a weight to the nodes or edges of the tree as another direction for further investigation. We conclude by highlighting the potential applications of our research in fields such as computational biology and graph theory. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. Furthermore, the model predicts that dust development will decrease gas recirculation in the disk's center and reduce the likelihood of stochastic particle recirculation. As a result, particle development presented in this research offers a possible explanation for observed particle behavior in protoplanetary disk systems. With additions to existing disk simulation codes, computational models can now incorporate particle development and settling, allowing for more accurate predictions of particle distribution in these areas. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time. Moreover, we show that these methods can generate robust models that accurately describe the systems' behaviors across different starting points. To further enhance model generalizability, we have also introduced a method for incorporating labeled data. Additionally, we explore the integration of SSMLearn with machine learning models, showcasing that these methods can be incorporated into optimization problems that minimize performance metrics, such as loss functions. These algorithms provide a foundation for conditional model generation and can be applied to various complex systems, facilitating the development of new methods that leverage these models in optimal ways. By providing multiple algorithm options and a publicly accessible dataset, we aim to stimulate research and further develop these methods in future work. All code is available at https://github.com/unixa/ssm-learning.

Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. A potential experimental implementation of these models is also discussed, involving optical-lattice-based investigations. This analytical study is accompanied by numerical data, including mass ratios, acceleration speeds, and potential sizes for both solitons, leading to feasible pathways for realizing self-accelerating solitons in binary BEC systems. This research may contribute to the development of versatile models for soliton theory. This study has been formally presented at the 29th International Conference on Integral Methods in Science and Engineering (IMSE2019). This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. SIMC 2.0's enhancements do not compromise its original security features, as proven through the extension of Chandran's security theories to include efficient protocols. To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, we open-source the SIMC 2.0 framework and provide the code for our customized solutions and experimental results. Additionally, we present an application of the efficient SIMC 2.0 framework in protecting a convolutional neural network used for image classification. As a result of these improvements, the modified SIMC 2.0 framework can serve as a robust and efficient foundation for the protection of various ML models and applications. As such, we hope that this research will inspire further innovation in secure ML research and provide a starting point for replication and extension of our findings. The source code for the customized solutions and experimental results is available at: https://github.com/songhai1996/SIMC-2.0.git. The modified code for the deep learning example is available at: https://github.com/songhai1996/SIMC-2.0.git/tree/master/example_cnn. The paper is also available at: https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1038.

Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The HI clouds in M101 rotate in sync with its main HI disk. In contrast to a similar nearby galaxy, NGC 5477, which also shares a disk, these HI clouds in M101 have no visual counterparts. Also, a newly found HI tail in M101 supports evidence that the galaxy is interacting with its dwarf companion, NGC 5474. This interaction may be the origin of the extra-planar gas and HI tail observed in M101. In this study, HI absorption has also been discovered in NGC 5474, indicating a gas rich structure surrounding this dwarf galaxy. In summary, HI detection in the M101 group has revealed various interactions between its member galaxies and their gas structures. Therefore, a spectral survey is recommended to analyze the atomic gas rich structures within this group, which could provide insights into the cosmological context of the central black hole growth relationship. Furthermore, the unique nature of the HI clouds in M101 deserves further attention, including potential supernovae populations within these clouds. The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. This technique does not rely on the structure of domain elements and can be closely linked to a method proposed by Hensel and Newman. We then demonstrate the implications of this method for certain specific domains and fields. In particular, we show that it enables the construction of an interesting type of ring with nonstandard properties and allows us to establish the connection between two well-known sets in the p-adic integers through a permutation. This, in turn, leads to an intriguing conjecture about the Diophantine equations with constant coefficients and a connection to a famous problem concerning the expression of integers as the sum of squares. Although our method for dividing a domain element into the sum of squared components can be applied directly, it also incorporates a subtle variation of another important problem. Thus, this advance not only addresses the basic question but also yields several interesting additional outcomes. We then review the well-known results for the basic question and provide the new insight for the domains (such as number domains with a prime factorization or global function domains with a local globalization theorem) where the established methods already ensure the desired outcome can be achieved. Therefore, the value of the new method lies in its generality and the novel applications it enables across these domains. Additionally, it introduces the concept of a minimal-length component, providing a direct solution to a long-standing challenge. This study is a follow-up to the work presented by the first author in his 2019 thesis. It incorporates the new perspective on the problem that has evolved over the past four years. This new approach has enabled the discovery of several interesting outcomes, which have not been previously published. It has also led to a fresh understanding of how to tackle the challenge across various fundamental domains and fields. We hope that this new insight will be beneficial in addressing the problem in an even broader range of contexts. We also hope that it will inspire further research in this area. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The algorithm's performance also exhibits robustness across different graph topologies and configuration settings. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. This concept is explored through analyses of previous studies, observations, and laboratory experiments. Furthermore, it is suggested that the recent discovery of large, persistent eddies in polar atmospheres may be a result of the bi-stable nature of rotating turbulence. These findings impose significant constraints on any theoretical models aimed at explaining the dynamics of rotating turbulent flows. Additionally, they raise fundamental questions about the properties and persistence of coherent structures found in such flows. Lastly, the study proposes that the spin parameter, previously identified as a key factor in wave turbulence, be redefined in terms of a Strouhal number and a Taylor number, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of bi-stable rotating turbulent flows. This new perspective is expected to be applicable across a broad range of rotating turbulent flows, from planetary core flows to planetary atmospheres and coastal reservoirs. Lastly, the study predicts that the development of high-resolution models will soon reveal the intricate bi-stable dynamics within planetary core flows. The study concludes by highlighting the need for further theoretical and computational models that can be tested against existing and future observations, along with laboratory experiments that can be used to bridge the scales. The study also proposes that the development of new numerical codes and simulation frameworks is necessary to tackle the complex bi-stable dynamics within planetary core flows. The study provides a starting point for a new area of research aimed at understanding the intricate bi-stable dynamics within planetary core flows and encourages collaboration among theoretical, computational, and experimental researchers within this field. The study is relevant to a broad range of rotating turbulent flows, from planetary core flows to atmospheric flows and coastal reservoirs, and provides a framework that can be used to understand the properties and persistence of coherent structures within these flows. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, a more detailed analysis also indicates that in addition to reducing crime, mental health treatment may also be preventing these individuals from entering the justice system in the future.  Therefore, it implies that a portion of the crime reduction can be attributed to a increased likelihood of these individuals being apprehended when they do return to the justice system.  The estimated financial benefit of providing this treatment to the evaluated group amounts to around $5000 per person, with expenses for providing such treatment totalling around $1500 per person.  Therefore, it appears that providing mental health treatment to these offenders is highly cost-effective and potentially even financially beneficial.  Furthermore, it also appears that court ordered mental health treatment may be reducing the likelihood of these offenders returning to the justice system in the future.  Therefore, it is worthwhile to conduct a longer term analysis as well as an analysis on violent crime specifically. To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This will mark the largest and most complex FPGA design installed at the CERN research facility. This paper provides an in-depth look at the design, performance, and operational capabilities of the jet FEX system and offers key takeaways for future FEX-style projects that involve complex algorithms and tight latency constraints. This work also paves the way for the deployment of enhanced jet triggers that will be critical for the ATLAS collaboration's future research endeavors. Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not
only DNR but also other avatar creation methods, demonstrating its superiority
through clear preferences and outstanding results on quantitative assessment metrics.
ANR enabled significantly improved visual stability, level of detail, and overall
plausibility in both static and dynamic scenes. The code and models for ANR are
open-source and ready for use at https://github.com/linguo/articulated_neural_rendering. To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Experimental results confirm the viability of this approach, showcasing better performance compared to current practices for synchronous learning and demonstrating the FedBuff algorithm's concurrent benefits. Furthermore, the study provides guidance on optimizing parameters to balance efficiency and convergence rate through numerical experiments. As the number of active clients continues to rise, the FedBuff algorithm's efficient asynchronous learning model is expected to play a significant role in the future of cross-device federated learning. The study's conclusions also contribute to a deeper understanding of the convergence properties of the FedBuff algorithm, making this research a significant contribution to cross-device federated learning. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our best model employed a combination of Czech and English data, employing a coarse-to-fine training style, and achieved a 13.3% Czech WER, representing a significant improvement over previous results. This approach has the potential to make a contribution to the development of ASR systems in resource-constrained languages. Full details of our method can be found in the paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.16254. We also made our code and data processing techniques available open-source at https://github.com/czechasr/czech-asr. We hope this will help advance the development of Czech ASR. Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance reported by LHCb in recent times.  Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. Moreover, the observed structure around $1.5$ GeV in $B^+ \to K^+K_S K_S$ spectrum, where $\rho^0(1450)$ cannot contribute due to Bose-Einstein statistics, is accounted for by an $S$-wave contribution alone.  The theoretical estimates of branching fractions and/or direct $CP$ asymmetries for $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$, $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ and $B^0 \to K^0 K^- K^+$ decays are presented for verification with upcoming experiments at LHCb and Belle-II.  Therefore, we recommend experimental validation through a more precise analysis of relevant data by these research colleagues.  Additionally, the proposed combination of multiple two-body contributions into a single complex spin state in $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm}K^+K^-$ spectrum is no longer supported.  Instead, it is suggested that the observed structure around $1.5$ GeV in this spectrum, where $\rho^0(1450)$ cannot contribute due to oscillation between $K^+K^-$ and $K_S K_S$, is accounted for by an $S$-wave contribution alone.  This research also offers an alternative explanation for the BaBar observation and encourages LHCb to verify this theoretically with relevant data. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This work has implications for a broader range of situations involving the expansion of materials broken down into pieces, such as dust expanding through space or clay breaking down in flowing water. It shows that in these cases, the structure of the material is shaped by the competition between its internal desire to reassemble and the force driving it apart. This knowledge can be used to improve the performance of materials like dust in solar panels or oil in refrigerant pipelines. It can also be applied to better understand other phenomena like the formation of cracks in drying paints or the destruction of sea ice in warming climates. Ultimately, this work highlights the significance of considering timescales in the study of material failure, which is a complex process influenced by both slow structural changes and fast dynamics. It demonstrates the value of using simple, easy-to-observe systems like particle rafts in the rigorous testing of theoretical models of material breakdown. It also shows that by successfully predicting the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments, these models can be used to gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental processes of material failure itself. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  This work's primary contribution is the development of a new SPGP-SARSA algorithm, and we also introduce the SPGP-TD method, both aimed at addressing the significant data collection challenges underwater robots face when learning through trial and error.  This work opens up new research paths and provides new techniques for tackling large data sets in online reinforcement learning contexts.  All of our project's code and data are openly available at https://github.com/angelotoledo/spgp_sarsa. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%. Notably, our method successfully reduced the gap between grades, especially between Mild and Critical, and effectively mitigated over-prediction of the Moderate grade. Moreover, our analysis into performance metrics across competition rules showed that our technique yielded the best results when both trainer and validator sets were used, albeit slightly inferior when only the trainer set was employed. Additionally, our study into balanced classes revealed that, despite achieving optimal results with a balanced model, there was a notable disparity between classes due to data collection limitations. As a result, our approach is not only effective but also highly relevant to real-world applications involving COVID-19 severity detection. The code for our solution has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.COM/AlibabaResearch/PaddleSeg/tree/2.1/examples/covid19. Meanwhile, the competition organizers have published evaluation codes and models on GitHub at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/CMC2021-Task1. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code and model weights are available for download at this link: https://github.com/ghrua/meta-gec.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but can severely distort results in other situations as demonstrated through practical applications. The simple techniques proposed are capable of mitigating the impact of rounding errors to some extent. The methods are versatile and can be applied to an broad range of rare event estimators. The research is an initial step aiming to raise awareness about the implications of releasing rounded statistical data and the need for tailored anti-poaching policies. The theoretical and practical findings are expected to facilitate discussions on this crucial issue. The software developed is available upon request. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, this EFX fairness condition holds in a weakened form, whereas we demonstrated an example of a mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations for any number of agents, where an allocation that is fair up to one good does not exist. Our investigation offers several generalizeable questions for further research. In our investigation, all mechanisms were assumed to be in the class of deterministic, integer-valued mechanisms. Additionally, our investigation focused on two-specific relaxation of envy-free allocation, namely allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX). Lastly, our investigation was limited to valuation functions that are additive and non-negative. As such, it remains to be determined whether similar results hold for other types of valuation functions or relaxation of envy-free allocation. Additionally, it remains to be determined whether similar results hold for mechanisms that are probabilistic or allow for allocations outside the domain of integer values. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. The code for our method has been made freely available for use by other researchers.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios. This innovative explanation framework for Random Forest models facilitates trust in their deployment. The developed project is readily available at https://github.com/mostofa-muhammed/Understanding-Random-Forest. The code has been integrated into the Python package scikit-learn as the 'RF' module. The project is further highlighted in our paper published in the 13th International Conference on Knowledge and Smart Data, 2021.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. By making the code and model available on open source platforms, we hope to stimulate the development of more effective unsupervised re-identification methods that can utilize large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video. At the very least, the dataset that we created consists of 30,000 distinct images spanning 1,436 identities, thereby surpassing the scale of currently available re-identification datasets by a significant margin. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. This model fits the data closely and reproduces the observed reactions to various scenarios. In contrast, when luck influences job success, participants are less eager to reduce the income gap and react differently to circumstances. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. The validity of our method is demonstrated through numerical simulation and experimental analysis of a single-mode laser resonator with mirror surfaces, as well as a vertical external-cavity surface-emitting laser with a flat mirror. The proposed entropy-based approach provides a versatile solution for assessing directional emission in various microcavity lasers. Additionally, we find that entropy is directly proportional to threshold current in both types of lasers, enabling a straightforward evaluation of directional emission using threshold current alone. Nevertheless, this correlation may not hold in lasers with complex structures or those with non-coherent emission modes. Overall, our method offers a comprehensive and versatile framework for evaluating the directional emission of microcavity lasers. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The comprehensive studies of our approach on the 3D MultiAgentHack challenges, iRail and stock portfolio optimization datasets demonstrate that our method delivers the best outcome compared to the state-of-the-art offline learning techniques for the agents. The successful implementation of the proposed approach is also accessible on the OpenMadMax platform for offline learning on multi-agent datasets. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Moreover, our analysis showcases the superiority of single-particle entanglement as a resource for quantum information processing tasks, notably the steering and robust generation of single-particle Bell diagonal states. Finally, our findings highlight the potential for single-particle entanglement to facilitate complex quantum operations based on the spread of the entangled wave function, underscoring the significance of single-particle entanglement in the field of quantum information science.

Despite the limitations, this research offers a potential path to achieving higher threshold depths in quantum learning machines utilizing multi-qubit gates, thereby enhancing the duration of accurate quantum processing. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Further enhancements result from training the GMM using information theoretic criteria, yet this introduces undue computational complexity. Initially, simple approaches like entropy minimization facilitate the GMM, yet more sophisticated techniques like weighted k-means produce superior codebook performance, but require excessive base station computations. Overall, the proposed system outperforms existing solutions, offering a balanced compromise between performance gains and system complexity. Evaluations utilizing real-world data sets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Moreover, numerical results illustrate the impact of various parameters on codebook performance. Interestingly, it is shown that, counterintuitively, the codebook's performance may actually decline when increasing the number of GMM components beyond a certain point due to decreased distance between entries in high-dimensional spaces. Also considered are systems with multiple antennas at both transmitting and receiving ends, but the focus remains on single-user applications, with extension to multi-user scenarios pending further investigation. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our framework also enables the prediction of characteristics of nuclear star clusters and their binary black hole mergers based on the behaviour of Population III binary remnants. This prediction is distinct from other models that also follow Population III binary remnants and may provide a way to test these models through the detection of Population III binary black hole mergers. GW190521 can already be seen as a potential landmark in this context. Instead of treating nuclear star clusters as a simple density profile, we incorporate details of their formation and development, which includes information about encounters with massive objects such as supernovae and the formation of compact binary systems.
