The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid controlled X-ray tube and direct digital synthesis technologies. This portable GRB simulator, which modulates an X-ray flux powered by up to 20 kV, demonstrates its capability of generating high-energy bursts. Before its launch in December 2020, both GECAM satellites were tested using this simulator, which produced short and long GRBs that were detected and analyzed by the onboard GECAM/GRDs. The results showed a strong consistency between the observed data and the programmed simulation functions, indicating excellent performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator. The successful development of this simulator ensures that comprehensive ground calibration and testing of the GRDs can be conducted, which is crucial for the activation and optimization of the detectors after launch. Additionally, it enables the simulation of various GRBs that can be used to trigger and test the onboard multi-level triggering and localization software of GECAM/GRDs. The simulator's ability to generate high-energy bursts also allows for the simulation of X-ray flares that can occur during the mergers of binary neutron star systems or the collapse of supercritical accretion discs. Therefore, this portable GRB simulator has played a key role in the development of GECAM/GRDs and ensured the readiness of the GECAM satellites for operation in 2022. The experience gained in developing this simulator has further enriched the GECAM team's understanding of GRB detection technology and has provided valuable training for the team in developing high-energy radiation detectors. The successful development of the portable GRB simulator has also benefited the development of other GRBD detection technologies in China. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2. These investigations are motivated by the recent breakthrough paper of P. Dukes and R. Zhao, further delving into the relationship between the semigroups of composition operators and the Volterra-type operators T_g on BMOA_p.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
As a result, researchers and developers can conduct in-depth comparisons between different virtual agents, demonstrating significant value in accelerating the development of advanced intelligent systems. 
We created TextWorldExpress by applying aggressive optimizations to original TextWorld simulations, employing a combination of techniques such as vectorizing grid operations, adapting simulation parameters, and leveraging hardware capabilities like parallel processing and fast random number generation. 
The resulting framework includes accelerated versions of three challenges—JumpWorld, CleanerWorld, and GroceryWorld—along with detailed instructions on incorporating its speed boosts into existing tests. 
As part of our research, we evaluated a range of search-based agents and mountain-car algorithms using the express versions, and the findings are comparable to previous results obtained with use of ordinary computers. 
The source code for TextWorldExpress is now available under the permissive MIT license to facilitate broad adoption. 
It is easy to incorporate the express versions into existing tests by following the provided instructions and switching to the accelerated versions. 
The research is also accompanied by comprehensive, reusable code for both accelerating the simulations and conducting similar optimizations on additional text-based games. 
Ultimately, TextWorldExpress represents a crucial step towards conducting more comprehensive, comparative studies between virtual agents by facilitating ongoing research in this field. 
As such, the community is invited to make use of TextWorldExpress, contribute their own results, and join the effort to accelerate more text-based games. 
The goal is to freely share all contributed results to facilitate ongoing discussion and debate.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. As a consequence, this research delivers a high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM network that can serve as a reliable foundation for the development of future enhanced LSTM architectures. Moreover, this work also provides a customized hardware framework that can be adapted for various compressed LSTM models, enabling them to leverage high-performance hardware acceleration for real-world applications. As a concrete demonstration, a video classification system is implemented utilizing the proposed FDHT-LSTM model and hardware accelerator, and the results indicate that it can achieve exceptional performance, efficiency, and accuracy when employed on embedded devices such as the Jetson TX2. As the research lays down an integrated algorithmic and hardware framework, it is anticipated that this will spark further innovation in the development of compact LSTM models and customized hardware accelerators, ultimately contributing to the broader adoption of LSTMs in practical sequence analysis applications. Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings. The associated code has been made publicly accessible.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The study also provides the model to the research community and future policy research through its open-source availability. The code can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/aiwachowski/asc- agency-based-model The model is a significant contribution to the PyPSA Python framework for Power System Analysis and is now integrated into the MESA agent-based modeling platform, and both models can be used separately for distinct research purposes. The model is particularly suited for investigating design options in ancillary services and electricity markets, an aspect that is currently hindered by the absence of computational methods for effective evaluation and policy advice. The model is comprised of multiple modules, each responsible for managing a distinct component of the electricity market, and is equipped with a multi-agent simulation feature that enables the exploration of different agent behaviors and the assessment of design options in a computationally efficient manner. The model is presented in a modular design that allows for straightforward integration of novel ancillary services and market structures, and is accompanied by a comprehensive performance indicator set that covers market operations, imbalances, pricing, and a novel pricing multiplier. The model is validated through a stylized simulation of a multi-period redispatch design

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly all interlinked with the change in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition, are responsible for such a shift in spectral weight.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that in V$_2$O$_3$, the metal-insulator transition is fundamentally driven by correlation between electrons, with the effect of these interactions playing a pivotal role in determining the transition's occurrence.  Our studies also offer a greater insight into understanding the electronic structure of systems with strong correlations, underscoring the significance of factoring in surface-related effects while interpreting experimental data collected through surface-sensitive techniques such as resistivity measurement, as this has significant implications for comprehending physical characteristics.  Our research offers a greater insight into understanding the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$, while also providing a comprehensive example of investigating the surface-related effects in materials with strong correlations.  In conclusion, a thorough analysis of the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination, which ultimately dictates the behavior of electrons at the surface.  Therefore, a comprehensive approach involving simultaneous investigation of surface structure, electron distribution, and the metal-insulator transition is imperative for a clear understanding of such transition in these materials. We anticipate that this phenomenon will result in a specific temporal pattern in the time-dependent density profile. Our results highlight the intricate interactions between different components of quantum double dark-soliton states and provide a theoretical basis for experimental observation of these phenomena. Furthermore, our studies may contribute to a better understanding of system behavior in states with multiple soliton structures. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  In addition, we observed that increasing temperature leads to a mixture of occupied and empty states in the center, revealing a non-equilibrium behavior.  We also studied the relaxation times of the two-energy-state system, and found that these times tend to lengthen at higher temperatures due to a decrease in non-luminescent processes, and subsequently, a decrease in temperature-driven empty-to-occupied transitions.  We believe that this research may pave the way for improving the visibility of the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, perhaps by increasing temperature to reduce competition from non-luminescent processes.  Furthermore, we propose that this system could serve as a model for studying atomic-scale physics in a strongly coupled environment at high temperatures.  We also suggest potential applications for this center, such as using it to study diamond materials, providing a reference point for comparing the properties of individual centers, and potentially enabling the detection of vacuum conditions based on the properties of the center.  We conclude by outlining potential areas for further research, including experiments conducted in controlled gas environments, studies of the center's properties when stimulated by light, and investigations of the center's spin coherence at high temperatures.  Ultimately, this center presents a valuable opportunity to explore the fundamental properties of diamond and fill the significant knowledge gap regarding its individual defects, particularly in vacuum and at high temperatures.  This center's unique properties also make it an ideal candidate for investigating atomic-scale physics in a strongly coupled environment at high temperatures, offering a promising potential for contributing to the development of quantum technology. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, we validate our findings numerically with experiments. Despite its generality, our analysis is expected to yield relevant theoretical and numerical insights for various applications, including sparse positive semidefinite programming, matrix completion, and low-rank matrix factorization. Keywords: matrix optimization, positive semidefinite cone, Riemannian geometry, landscape analysis, geodesic convexity, strong convexity.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering. These findings demonstrate that even a small number of Ising agents can exert a substantial influence on the system in an environment where the vast majority of agents follow the voter model dynamics. This research was conducted with the purpose of understanding the phenomenon of critical slowing down observed in a similar mixed-island model, where domain growth theory has been applied to analyze the effects of contrasted dynamics within the same network. This study could contribute to a better understanding of how minority opinion agents may influence a majoritarian society and vice versa. This research also highlights the unique properties of an interface in an out-of-equilibrium system. The behavior of the interface, characterized by the magnetization and correlation length, diverges at the same temperature as susceptibility does, which is a characteristic shared with the pure Ising model despite the failure of detailed balance for a significant range of concentrations. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Finally, we compare our model's predictions to existing studies and the available data, with further research needed to confirm our findings. Despite the complexity of this problem, our analysis demonstrates that a simple model can effectively capture the key processes involved in virus spread from droplets, making it a valuable tool for further analysis and potential applications. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of considering the interplay between gravity, evaporation, and diffusion in understanding the infection spread from virus-carrying droplets. While our analysis is specific to COVID19, it may also be applicable to other respiratory viruses that spread through contaminated droplets. As the COVID19 pandemic has primarily been transmitted through aerosolized droplets, our study emphasizes the necessity of further research into the behavior of these virus-carrying droplets in various environments to effectively combat the infection's spread. As a simple model, our analysis can facilitate numerical computations, whereas a comprehensive investigation involving complex simulations would be necessary for more refined models. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework. This research represents a crucial step towards establishing a set of best practices for reliable solution-proving using neural networks. In addition, future improvements are anticipated to facilitate even broader adoption of NNs across the broader engineering and scientific community. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases. The source code is available online at https://github.com/ondoro/Range-Reliable-ConvNet.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. All code and data are freely accessible at https://github.com/zhuegg/multiling-uws.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The proposed framework is readily applicable to various dataset scenarios and delivers a notable advancement in robust training from inaccurate labels. Furthermore, we introduce the issue of dataset state tracking, focusing on inferring the label noise distribution instead of directly predicting actual labels, and explore possible future directions for ASSIST to tackle this newly proposed challenge. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A tentative proposal is made to amend the model by integrating a new feature that takes into account the influence of transportation systems on the movement of individuals and the spread of unrest, which in turn could be applied to better model the syndemic spread of riots in Santiago. A numerical implementation of this modified model was developed and tested on Santiago's subway layout, resulting in a plausible simulation of the city's rioting patterns. A brief discussion is also presented on potential methods to refine and validate this model using actual data from Santiago's riots. Furthermore, the implications are considered for other major cities with underground rail networks. The code developed for this project is freely accessible online. In addition, possible connections are explored between this research and other related studies, such as the epidemiological model combined with spatial mobility data to analyze the spread of unemployment in nineteenth-century London. Lastly, possible extensions to this project are proposed, including the integration of additional mechanisms affecting rioting activity and the application of machine learning to better model agents' behavior. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. However, we also identify potential limitations of the model's performance when observing this line, particularly when considering variations in dust content. We are studying a critical boundary that involves breaking down real polynomials into the sum of squares of other real polynomials, specifically those that don't equal zero. This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and we have already successfully identified the complete description for some specific cases with low degrees in a small number of variables. However, more complex cases with more variables or higher degree polynomials remain to be fully understood and there is currently very limited knowledge on them. Using an assumption from D. Eisenbud, M. Green, and J. Harris, we have obtained new restrictions for the number of decomposed polynomials and the matrix dimensions in this context. These new restrictions particularly improve our understanding for homogeneous quartic polynomials in 5 variables and they match a recent confirmed case in this context. Lastly, combining both theoretical calculations and computational techniques, we have obtained specific examples and counterexamples to further analyze the general applicability of G. Blekherman's findings and we have proven that the established bounds are indeed reachable. Additionally, our research has led to a description of the boundary of this problem through a new geometric interpretation and we have derived the explicit formulas for the dimension estimates. All of these results and insights have enabled us to resolve the original problem and its related questions positively.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. Additionally, we predict that SHOWS will exhibit unique photoemission spectra under linear dichroism, which can be used to identify showstones. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Furthermore, to facilitate widespread adoption, we made the code and data publicly available to support further research in FedSA. As organizations continue to invest heavily in sophisticated neural networks, it is imperative to explore more efficient ways to leverage their existing expertise to achieve greater community gains. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Furthermore, we explore and evaluate various theoretical frameworks that attempt to explain grid cells' underlying mechanisms and functional roles within the context of the wider spatial navigation network. Finally, we speculate on potential future directions for grid cell research, given its significance for the broader field of spatial navigation. Despite significant progress made to date, the exact underlying mechanisms and functional roles of grid cells within the parahippocampal-hippocampal network remain poorly understood and require continued research focus.

As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. Furthermore, they have demonstrated the sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing two types of propanediol isomers, revealing that certain conditions produce a significantly increased yield of methyl ions. Simulation results indicate that this increase results from an optimal molecular alignment on the droplet's surface in one isomer, paving the way for the observation of charge dynamics and chemical reactions within droplets. Additionally, this study has introduced reaction nanoscopy as a versatile tool applicable to various droplet sizes, charges, and surrounding environments, enabling the exploration of complex chemical systems and offering a new perspective on droplet chemistry. This study provides a groundbreaking example of this novel approach, offering a new perspective on droplet chemistry. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. In addition, comprehensive experiments are conducted to examine the impact of different components of the proposed method on its performance. Furthermore, strategic considerations to mitigate the necessity for large-scale training are also explored to ensure potential clinical applicability. As a result, this work represents a significant advancement in the use of multi-scale graph representations for cancer subtyping and paves the way for similar investigations in other medical applications. All code and data associated with this project are available for access at https://github.com/ghulam-eiman/HACT-Net.

We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. They serve as a crucial tool for developing probabilistic methods involving random error scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our symmetric error model by illustrating connections to other coding theories, including the Kerdock code, optimal binary codes, and certain types of linear codes over finite fields. We also examine the phenomenon of code rate growth in a symmetric error environment and discuss potential connections to the zoo of good asymptotic binary codes. Lastly, we outline potential applications and future directions for our findings.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Therefore, SN~2020jfo may represent a transitional type, linking SNe~II with plateau phases to SNe~P. Observations of SN~2020jfo's host galaxy revealed a gas-rich, dwarf irregular galaxy with an overall low metal content. However, the analysis of the SN~2020jfo's spectrum suggested a more moderately metal content in the region surrounding the explosion site. The host galaxy's low metal content, combined with the relatively large progenitor mass, make SN~2020jfo an interesting candidate for further study in comparing its properties with other low-luminosity SNe~II. SN~2020jfo's explosion and evolution into a supernova offer valuable insights into the physics of these distant cosmic events. Nonetheless, more observations and analyses are required to fully comprehend the nature and characteristics of this remarkable hydrogen-rich Type II supernova. SN~2020jfo's data, including spectra and photometry, is available at the Weizmann Interactive Telescope (WIT) Data Base and can be accessed through the AAVSO Archive. The team welcomes additional analyses and interpretations of the data in order to enhance the understanding of this significant astronomical event.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. With MuLE, we estimate that the number of required image sensors could be reduced by a factor of ~30 in such applications. A prototype MuLE for the MAXI scanner on board the International Space Station is currently in development, and we hope this new optical system will also enhance the sensitivity of future wide-field X-ray monitors. Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Furthermore, our analysis on the MAPS dataset reveals that employing an instrument-specific baseline reduces the performance gap between low-rank factorization methods and top-performing deep learning models. This instrument-specific baseline serves as a key component in our proposed semi-supervised model, resulting in an enhanced low-rank factorization approach. Nonetheless, our findings indicate that low-rank factorization methods alone are insufficient for accurate piano transcription. Nevertheless, this study provides valuable insights into developing more effective music transcription methods and suggests several possible directions for research and development. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These novel numerical tools will serve as critical components for our future numerical experiments aimed at investigating the quasi-static evolutionary processes in rotating stars. 

Additionally, we have constructed a rotating star model with a substantial magnetic field, based on the ideal MHD formulation, using the same approach mentioned above. This includes the integration of magnetized pressure and magnetic stress components into the balance equation, along with the magnetic induction equation, all solved through our Lagrangian methodology. This novel numerical tool will enable us to study the interactions between magnetic fields and stellar material in rotating stars. 

Our approach has several key advantages, including the ability to accommodate complex internal structures, generate configurations of optimal stability, and produce precise configurations consistent with given external gravitational and thermal fields. This method also offers enhanced flexibility, allowing for various physical parameters and fundamental equations to be easily substituted or modified. This method is particularly suited for rotational problems, and could also be adapted for use in Eulerian formulations.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Compared to traditional active learning methods, our approach also eliminates the need to select final model ensemble members manually. Our code and data are openly available for replication and further research at the specified URL.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. Furthermore, we present methods to enhance the training process and mitigate the impact of noise on the network's performance. Despite being initial exploratory findings, these results lay the groundwork for further development in deep learning applications involving gravitational wave data, and highlight the potential for deep neural networks to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of signal processing in future detectors. We anticipate that incorporating these algorithms into online detection pipelines will enhance the likelihood of detecting neutron star and binary neutron star events, and facilitate timely multi-messenger observations in future astrophysical events. Alongside this, we suggest incorporating a neutron star merger identifier on the Gravitational Wave Observatory's public website, to engage the public in the multi-messenger experience and facilitate access to this research's results. Ultimately, we are making the code and data used in this study openly available, and invite contributions in this emerging field of gravitational wave research. We are also offering to collaborate with electromagnetic researchers to leverage these algorithms in the analysis of future multi-messenger events. We hope that, in conjunction with the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, this research will contribute to a greater understanding of neutron star events, including their dense matter state, and facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of these phenomena through multi-messenger astronomy. We intend to deploy this identifier on the Gravitational Wave Observatory's public website, to engage the public in the multi-messenger experience and facilitate access to this research's results.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving better overall Micro-F1 score and outshining existing state-of-the-art models when handling the critical issue of overlapping entities.

Ultimately, our study successfully validated the potential of the proposed system to effectively identify and extract vital social determinants of health information from clinical notes, a crucial development with the potential to enhance clinical care and monitoring. However, there are concerns regarding error propagation, necessitating future research to further optimize entity extraction, particularly when encountering entities with complex meaning and a scarcity of available data. The source code for this study has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github/sdoe. Despite the current limitations, we believe this study lays the groundwork for the development of clinical care and monitoring systems powered by social determinants of health information and lays the foundation for future optimization techniques. 

In addition to entity extraction, future work should also focus on incorporating existing clinical patient data into the system to ensure a comprehensive understanding of patients' social determinants of health. Ultimately, this study has the potential to pave the way for the development of clinical care and monitoring systems powered by social determinants of health information.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. This research offers a methodological framework that can be applied to analyze the interplay between urban diversity, mobility, and counterfactual analysis through artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques. This research also lays the groundwork for investigating the economic and social consequences of diversity of urban encounters and moving beyond correlation-based analysis to explore more intricate relationships between variables. This research itself is an example of a diverse urban encounter, presenting a holistic framework that combines data-driven insights with theoretical frameworks to further the discussion on this topic. Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address these concerns, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, adolescents, schools, and medical centers, also applicable to pre-5G scenarios. This methodology is then applied to two real-world case studies. Findings indicate that as 5G adoption increases, so too will the exposure from 5G cellular towers. However, international safety guidelines still remain unaffected by these findings. Interestingly, children's and teenagers' exposure rates to 5G resemble the average exposure experienced by the broader population, whereas exposure within schools and medical centers can sometimes be lower than average. Furthermore, it is observed that when accounting for building attenuation and assuming 5G's maturity, its exposure rates significantly surpass pre-5G exposure. Nonetheless, more research is needed to thoroughly understand the exposure characteristics of 5G across various scenarios. Additionally, there is a necessity to revisit and adapt safety guidelines in accordance with emerging 5G exposure trends. As international standards for evaluating 5G exposure are yet to be established, a proposed approach is to adapt the ISO 14185 method for determining exposure from 5G base stations, while also incorporating new 5G specifications, such as large antenna arrays, and incorporating the findings from the presented case studies. By adopting this approach, a more accurate assessment of 5G exposure can be made, thus enabling a review of safety guidelines, especially for locations with uncertain or variable occupancy. As a result, this work aims to contribute to the discussion surrounding 5G exposure and its potential implications for building a more sustainable and responsible mobile network ecosystem. As mobile networks continue to evolve at a rapid pace, it is becoming increasingly essential to assess exposure from these networks with equal pace, mostly through numerical evaluations as seen in this work, to guarantee a holistic review of safety guidelines that considers the unique characteristics of each generation. Ultimately, this work's approach can be applied across various mobile networks to ensure a responsible development of these systems. As such, it is hoped that this work's contributions will inform the discussion around exposure from these networks, contribute to the review of safety guidelines, and guide the development of mobile networks in a more sustainable and responsible manner. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Furthermore, the system's modules can be easily adapted to accommodate various sensor setups, proving the flexibility of this holistic navigation approach. Additionally, an analytical comparison between cooperative and individual sensor performance in multi-layer zoning is provided, highlighting the benefits of cooperative navigation. Meanwhile, a module's sensitivity to sensor data loss and its recovery mechanism from temporary failures have also been explored, demonstrating the system's ability to adapt in harsh environments. A pioneering acoustic sensor error correction method, inspired by the shape-matching principle found in nature, has been introduced and shown to enhance the system's performance when sensors encounter irregular surfaces. A comprehensive discussion surrounding potential future improvements and a summary of the presented research serve as a foundation for advocating the use of cooperative navigation in complex indoor environments. A comparative analysis between cooperative and individual sensor performance in multi-layer zoning has been statistically evaluated, revealing a notable improvement of around 40% in the former. Moreover, the system has demonstrated an impressive ability to recover from temporary failures, with a sensitivity of approximately 20 seconds. Lastly, the proposed shape-matching inspired sensor error correction method has yielded a striking 30% reduction in errors. Consequently, this groundbreaking research provides a robust foundation for the development of a collaborative navigation system, capable of managing complex indoor environments and adapting to irregular surfaces, surface obstructions, and moving objects, thereby paving the way for the use of acoustic sensors in harsh indoor settings. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution strategy. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our solutions with numerical examples. Moreover, we analyze how security decoding order performance relates to system parameters including the number of users and multiplexing gains. Finally, we investigate the potential of our suboptimal solution in real-world applications. Additionally, we find that our suboptimal solution can handle a large number of users and high multiplexing gains without difficulty. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Kopczyński (ICALP 2006) hypothesized that prefix-independence in half-positional winning conditions leads to closed unions. Contrary to this hypothesis, we demonstrate that such conditions are not finite union-closed over limited scenarios. To disprove this hypothesis, we define a new set of bi-positional winning conditions known as 'energy conditions,' specifically tailored for totally ordered groups. Furthermore, we present an instance of two conditions within this new set whose union is not positionally significant. Building upon this finding, we theorize that any condition with this independence property shares similarities with energy conditions, especially those defined on totally ordered groups over cyclical sequences. Lastly, we formulate the 'Energy Condition Hypothesis,' which would imply that all such conditions have unions that are independent of partial sequences. To support this hypothesis, we offer an analogue of Kopczyński's theorem for bi-positional games over cyclical sequences within totally ordered groups. Finally, we anticipate that further research is necessary to achieve a broader generalization of these results.

In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Our evaluation will involve two different mesh sizes, with a focus on a method employing a partitioned approach with a reduced basis size. To assess the accuracy of these methods, we'll compare them to a fully integrated solution on a small mesh. Notably, our research finds that both reduction approaches can accurately capture the dynamic behavior of an FSI problem with a relatively small number of basis elements, especially when using a monolithic approach, and that the method employing a partitioned approach with a reduced basis size can significantly decrease the computational costs while maintaining a comparable level of accuracy. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Additionally, this work provides an overview of the strong normalization proofs in relation to the development of dependently typed programming languages and then discusses potential applications of legacy proof code to the ongoing research in programming languages and type theory. This survey is part one of a broader examination exploring the influence of the Calculus of Constructions on the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic, featuring an in-depth analysis of the core theory itself. We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. With this modified understanding of the bulk-point limit, the model can accurately reproduce scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space. The proposed approach is expected to yield comparable results for twist-three operators in AdS$_4$ times S$^3$. The explicit expression for the two-loop anomalous dimension of the diquark operator is also presented, showing excellent agreement with independent results derived via perturbation theory. The method can be applied to calculate the anomalous dimensions of other twist-four operators by scaling the spin of the diquark operator. The comprehensive analysis provides a robust foundation for exploring other channels and operators. The extended bulk-limit interpretation offers a new perspective on the relationship between AdS and flat-space physics. The simple model of zigzag integrals effectively captures the leading logarithmic properties of gravitational amplitudes in various channels, indicating the fundamental role of these ingredients in the context of AdS amplitudes. This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient. Overall, FourierMask provides a compelling instance segmentation approach that offers both high-quality mask generation and remarkable object detection applications. Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms. To test this new perspective, we ran the SAIL4J 3D radiative transfer simulator with a simplified core model and observed significant reductions in computing time. These findings could lead to further enhancements of tomographic reconstruction algorithms, ultimately enabling more accurate and efficient 3D cloud reconstruction from space-based observations. By acknowledging the existence of cloud cores and streamlining computations, we may one day be able to accurately map three-dimensional cloud properties from space. Due to the complexities involved, a fully autonomous 3D cloud tomography algorithm cannot be implemented at this time; rather, it is suggested to refine existing 2D retrieval algorithms to handle two-component cloud scenarios. By recognizing the veiled cloud core and streamlining computations, we can leverage machine learning to incorporate this physics-based insight, potentially leading to significant advancements in cloud tomography in the future.
