We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. However, negative frequency variations allow for increased transmission at higher densities (six times the critical density), producing a highly stable and persistent electrostatic field behind the target and significant ion acceleration in opposite directions due to the electron void. Additionally, our experiment features an auxiliary thin layer with low density, situated behind the main target layer. Ions from the auxiliary layer can be efficiently accelerated into a mono-energetic beam by the electrostatic field generated in the main target under interaction with a negatively frequency-modulated, highly intense laser pulse, achieving protons with maximum energies of around 100 MeV when subjected to specific optimal conditions involving a 10-fs, intensively Gaussian pulse with 8.5 times ten to the power of twenty watts per square centimeter peak intensity. Our experimental findings demonstrate the potential of sub-wavelength targets for the development of novel particle acceleration technologies. However, the suitability of such targets for thin-layer target normalization, relied on upon accurate modeling of the target's response to complex laser pulses. Moreover, further research is needed to address challenges related to target materials and limits of stable ion acceleration due to ion return currents. Ultimately, this approach faces the difficulty of distinguishing between ions from the auxiliary layer and those from the main target following a single shot, although the latter can be achieved on average basis by manipulating target properties and the laser in an appropriate manner. Despite these limitations, our study offers a framework for exploring ion acceleration in an electrostatic field behind a sub-wavelength target through proper target normalization, in addition to illustrating the peculiar characteristics of density-modulated laser pulses and the advantages of using negatively frequency-modulated pulses. Furthermore, this study provides a foundation for further investigation into the capabilities and limitations of this novel approach to ion acceleration. It also highlights the significance of a thorough understanding of the target's response to complex laser pulses, achieved via precise modeling, in realizing the full potential of this technology. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Additionally, our study reveals that nitrogen defects are more stable in the anatase phase of TiO2, whereas carbon defects prefer the rutile phase.  Finally, we predict that both carbon and nitrogen defects will undergo lattice relaxation upon substitutional substitution, with the latter resulting in bond breaking and formation of dimer with oxygen.  This study provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of carbon and nitrogen defects within TiO2, and offers potential pathways for optimizing photocatalytic properties.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Additionally, I highlight that in the case of elastic top-quark pair production, limits on the cross-section of $\sigma_\mathrm{elastic}\approx 0.9$ fb with on order 10 sigma confidence can be obtained with as little as 10 inverse picobarns of data. This represents a crucial contribution to the understanding of top-quark pair production in a purely elastic process. This analytical approach will also be relevant to future experiments such as the LHC at its high-energy phase or future hadron colliders.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics. Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is partially achieved by non-thermal pressure and the dissipation of turbulent energy. X-ray emission line mapping, essential for studying ICM turbulence, is complicated by the lack of high-resolution spectroscopy. Future X-ray detectors like the X-IFU on Athena will enable thorough investigations of ICM turbulence across multiple scales. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. When analyzing these quantities, measurements are constrained by instrumental uncertainties and the inherent variability in cosmic observations. Here, the formalism established in a previous paper is expanded to account for the statistical uncertainty in line diagnostics, specifically structure functions. Statistical variance contributes to total variance in several ways, influenced by the detector's geometry, spatial binning, and the characteristics of turbulent fields. These terms hold significant importance for studying turbulence at smaller scales. A demonstration is conducted for the X-IFU using a simulated turbulent velocity map of a galaxy cluster resembling Coma. Results indicate excellent agreement with theoretical formulas for structure function estimation and its associated variance. These derived expressions can be applied to any X-ray measurement of turbulent structure functions and provide a framework for optimizing future instrumentation and observational strategies. Furthermore, this framework enables a comparison of outstanding challenges in gaseous galaxy clusters with turbulent structure functions, effectively providing a roadmap for achieving robust line diagnostics. Ultimately, this implies that a 1 ksec observation of the Coma cluster with X-IFU will yield a total variance of approximately 1000 km^2, a benchmark that will likely require a combination of advanced instrumental capabilities and sophisticated data processing to achieve the desired metric accuracy across the entire field-of-view. However, achieving this goal will significantly facilitate a thorough investigation of ICM turbulence in galaxy clusters like Coma when Athena is launched in 2028. Nonetheless, even with the X-IFU's proposed configuration, the challenge of studying turbulence down to the smallest scales will likely require an optimization of operational parameters to balance structure function variance by adjusting exposure time, particle count per pixel, and background subtraction. Consequently, a rigorous simulation process is needed to inform strategic decisions on how to best study ICM turbulence in future X-ray missions. Finally, the methods presented in this work can be applied to any X-ray detector that provides line diagnostics, enabling a theoretical understanding of structure function estimation and its associated variance. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Our findings also consider Ramsey numbers in defined classes and the $\lambda$ value for specific cycle graphs. Lastly, we mention a technique that may be applied to further investigate upper density problems within Ramsey theory.

Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Furthermore, we have established a notable advantage of our eye-only system when compared to their facial image counterparts. Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. In this work, measurement protocols that efficiently utilize multiple degrees of freedom are also explored, showcasing the potential for further noise mitigation. A discussion on the limitations of our study and the potential applications of this research are also presented.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. However, it's also worth noting that the degree of polarization could be further optimized through the adjustment of pre-conditioning parameters in experiments. In addition, our simulation shows that an extremely intense linearly polarized laser can effectively generate a massive number of positrons with notable polarization properties, offering promising implications for a wide range of applications. The achievable charge of positrons could be substantially enhanced by utilizing a thicker, but still extremely dense, target due to the unique properties of positrons in intense laser fields. The generation of positrons with notable polarization properties provides a potential new source of polarized positrons, capable of addressing the positron deficit issue in certain materials, such as helium. In addition, this could also enable the study of matter-antimatter pairing and the potential production of antihydrogen. Furthermore, the effective generation of a massive number of positrons with notable polarization properties may also give rise to a novel application involving the generation of intense, polarized electron or positron beams. In this regard, the interaction between high-power lasers and dense targets may offer a feasible new approach for the creation of such beams, with potential uses in a variety of experiments,

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Additionally, this research introduces the concept of distended groups, characterized by a large, moderately-sized subgroup with a high order and significant depth, and demonstrates that such groups have a diameter that scales polynomially. It also proves that the symmetric group Sn can be expressed as the union of multiple arXiv classes, and that the projective general linear group PGL(2,q) has a significant abelian subgroup close to its highest order for small values of q. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the group PSL(2,Q_q)[Q^2] has two significant, moderately-sized subgroups with high orders and significant depths, particularly when q is an infinite, positively ordered field. It is also shown that the group Sn has multiple conjugacy classes of the same size for infinitely many values of n. It is also proven that a group G has a diameter of at most n if and only if it has a generating set S of size at most n, and it demonstrates the polynomial diameter conjecture for Coxeter groups and certain 3-dimensional solvable groups that are not torus groups. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries. We graphically represented these boundaries in the form of a magnetic energy ratio map. This finding suggests the possibility of finding stable magnetic fields of this type in stars with stable interiors over long periods of time. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and higher-dimensional models and anticipate it to contribute positively to further research into the renormalization group in quantum field theories. Nous présentons une stratégie innovante consistant à considérer les équations de flux comme des équations de conservation présentes dans la dynamique des fluides et proposons l'adaptation de méthodes numériques avancées issues de cette théorie pour résoudre les équations de flux, en particulier pour comprendre l'apparition de comportements analytiques non triviaux. Notre approche facilite la compréhension des flux de renormalisation qui pourraient être irréversibles. Nous explorons l'application de ce cadre aux modèles de dimension une et aux modèles de dimensions supérieures. Ce travail ouvert la voie à de futures recherches sur les équations de flux en théories de champs quantiques. Ce work a été financé par l'ANR under contract number ANR-17-CE29-0026. Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options. Unlike traditional search engines that return random results based on queries, Pied Piper's unique approach ensures ordered results displaying the most suitable matches first. We've tested our concept through a practical experiment and developed the underlying technology as an open-source framework, which is now available for public use. By sharing our findings and source code, we hope to inspire further development and improvements, ultimately creating a community-driven music search engine that exceeds the capabilities demonstrated here. A preliminary implementation of Pied Piper can be accessed at [pii.ped.pie](http://pii.ped.pie). A detailed description of our approach, including the underlying algorithms and source code, is available at [our research repository](https://github.com/pedrograca/pied-piper). A paper detailing our concept and results has been submitted to the 13th Audio/Video-based, Cross-modal Understanding and Applications Workshop, concurrently taking place at ICML 2021.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we observe a substantial increase in the mass of cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud compared to similar regions at greater distances, indicating that core mass grows with the distance from the Sun.  This discovery is consistent with the idea that core mass is dictated by the density of the parental molecular cloud rather than the process of star formation itself.  We also find evidence suggesting that high-density infrared dark clouds have a higher ratio of protostellar cores to starless cores, especially in cores with masses greater than 100 solar masses, indicating that dense IRDCs may serve as a primary site for massive star formation.  Finally, we offer a hypothesis to explain the prevailing view that massive star formation is driven by massive prestellar cores, suggesting that the most massive cores formed during the early stages of the universe's evolution were indeed massive in proportion to their surrounding environments, thus giving the appearance of a causal relationship between massive cores and massive star formation.  However, we propose that the process of massive core formation is governed by the density of the parental cloud rather than the results of star formation itself, offering the Dragon infrared dark cloud as concrete evidence for this hypothesis.  We also offer the hypothesis that massive star formation is linked to massive cores as support for the proposed mass function of the new generation of stars, which we believe will provide a valuable tool for analyzing the origins of massive star formation across various galaxies.  Finally, we suggest that the unique conditions of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, characterized by high densities and moderate velocities, may indicate its location on the edge of a spiral arm or bar.  We further propose that the prevalence of massive star formation in this region could be attributed to the spiral arm or bar's influence on the density and structural properties of the surrounding molecular cloud,

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Moreover, we find that using contextual information yields higher accuracy rates across almost all feature engineering methods tested. Additionally, some techniques like kernel-based methods and neural networks prove sensitive to specific parameters and may not consistently achieve optimal results. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive examination of classification approaches for 3D LiDAR data, offering a foundation for further exploration and more complex scenarios involving multi-modal sensor data. The associated code is publicly accessible for replication and extension. The used dataset and evaluation results are included in the supplementary material. The approach that worked best in our study is available as a standalone classification tool on GitHub.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. Additionally, this paper explores the implications of these operators for the reconstruction of zonal functions and provides an alternative approach using a Fourier-Bessel expansion. The proposed method has the advantage of operating directly with the function's defining integral equation, bypassing the dependence on space dimension. The resulting operator can be interpreted as a radial analog of the classical half-differentiation operator used in functions defined on the real line. The method also offers an interesting connection to the classical Fourier-Bessel expansion, enabling the positive definite function to be expressed as a series of Bessel functions, and further extends the concept of half-differentiation to the context of zonal functions on the sphere. The method is robust and feasible for computational purposes, as demonstrated by its application to the construction of a radial positive definite function associated with a fractional power. The paper also highlights the connection to the recent work by C. R. Remus, S. R. L. Clausen, and H. M. Kim on the characterisation of zonal functions in terms of Gegenbauer polynomials, and provides an alternative proof of the associated recursion formula for zonal functions. The proposed method has the additional benefit of clarifying the role of Lagrange's formula for differentiation and integration, as well as the construction of a system of functions that is orthogonal with respect to a varying positive definite function. The method's simplicity and the use of a system of functions that is orthogonal with respect to a varying positive definite function enable the extension of these results to the multiple dimension context. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the neutrino-UHECR spatial correlations. Additionally, the studies reveal UHECR-neutrino spatial connections and discuss possible interpretations. With increased data sets, the significance thresholds for the analyses have been tightened by at least a factor of thirty. To facilitate replication and further exploration, the neutrino and UHECR datasets used in the analyses, along with the related papers, are openly available at this link: https://github.com/ANTARENEutrino/UHECR-Neutrino-Correlations. Consequently, more sensitive searches utilizing combined datasets from future experiments such as Pierre Auger Upgrade, Extremely Large Telescopes, Square Kilometre Array, and next-generation neutrino detectors like KM3Net and ORCA, which will significantly enhance the sensitivity by at least a factor of thirty again, are anticipated to provide significant insights into the UHECR origin problem. Consequently, the current analysis faces statistical limitations that will be vastly outweighed by theoretical and systematic uncertainties with improved searches. Nonetheless, the methods proposed here will still be useful in future analyses. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. We've also derived an expression for average dissipated energy in terms of an equilibrium correlation energy, revealing that it serves as a fundamental thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, we provide a general framework that enables calculation of the dissipated energy in other scenarios, such as systems connected by irreversible processes. As a specific example, we show that the dissipated energy is directly proportional to the square of the temperature difference in a system consisting of two thermal reservoirs connected via a resistor. Finally, we propose that the proposed method for calculating the dissipated energy could be used as a thermometric technique to measure temperature changes in systems subject to irreversible processes. As such systems are common in various areas, understanding the dissipated energy in this context can provide valuable insights into the underlying thermodynamic processes taking place. Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  We believe that our research will motivate the scientific community to explore the design of computer-supported collaborative learning environments that can identify and respond to curiosity in real-time.  This is achievable because the variables that influence curiosity are observable and can be anticipated in advance.  Such an investigation is crucial because a computer system that can foster curiosity may be an effective way to promote curiosity more fundamentally.  In the long run, this is essential for developing computer systems that can motivate a desire to learn and develop a love for learning and, ultimately, a desire to continue learning throughout a person's life.  This is the key to surviving and thriving in a future where constant learning will be increasingly essential.  We are exploring the possibilities of extending this research to study the development of computer systems that can learn to identify and respond to curiosity in a more fundamental way, i.e., without being programmed to do so, by incorporating ideas from the study of social learning in animals, particularly monkeys, as identified in the work of Tomasello and colleagues.  This is an extremely challenging problem, but we are convinced that it is essential to designing computer systems that can effectively deal with the complexities of human learning and development and, ultimately, to creating computer systems that can learn from humans in a collaborative learning setting. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research is further underscored by an open-source implementation that is freely accessible. This implementation not only facilitates the evaluation of these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes by providing a flexible toolkit that is simple to use but also offers a versatile platform that is easily integrable within more complex applications and can be used to explore a broader class of Gaussian processes that are defined through similar stochastic partial differential equations. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, this approach reduces the coverage gap between theoretical maximum coverage and actual coverage by at least 27.2%. Our optimization technique achieves a coverage optimization ratio of 1.42 times better than the baseline strategy, and a reliability optimization ratio of 1.35 times better than the baseline strategy in different scenario variations. Our findings also highlight the importance of incorporating urban road topology in data analysis for mobile sensing. Our approach and research questions can serve as a foundation for future mobile sensing studies in various transportation networks. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. We demonstrate that a detailed study of J/ψ decay into invisible matter has the potential to provide valuable insights into the nature of dark matter and may even reveal the existence of light sterile neutrinos, assuming their masses remain within certain cosmologically allowed ranges. Consequently, a thorough investigation of J/ψ decay into invisible matter is crucial for a deeper comprehension of these fundamental components of our universe. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Additionally, we show that our new methods have similar order conditions to existing first derivative linear methods and Nordieck-type SGLMs when using uniform grids. This research aims to provide a starting point for further exploration of variable stepsize SGLMs. We also propose an implicit Runge-Kutta method that facilitates variable stepsize SGLM constructions and prove its order conditions. Through numerical experiments and theoretical analysis, we verify that these new methods converge at order p when solving non-stiff problems on uniform grids, and at order q=p when solving stiff problems on uniform and non-uniform grids.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attribution patterns or characteristics of manipulable data, thus enabling the identification of suspicious scores with higher effectiveness. Our findings are relevant not only to the specific autoscoring models investigated but also to any other scoring systems developed using similar techniques. Furthermore, our detection-based protection solutions are applicable to a broad range of other sensitive machine learning models that are difficult to understand and analyze in complex scenarios. All code and data used in this research are available at https://github.com/ghrua/Autoscoring-Probing.

A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies. Additionally, the advantages of microbial pesticides over chemical pesticides are highlighted through an economic analysis, which takes into account the costs of production, application, and the nematode itself. A dynamic pricing approach is also implemented to determine the optimal price for the nematode based on its marginal benefit, which is calculated through a benefit-cost ratio that considers the long-term consequences of nematode application. This results in the company profit also exhibiting a benefit-cost ratio, which is optimal at the point of highest revenue, making it a suitable measure for decision-making. This research provides theoretical and practical insights into the optimal application and pricing of microbial pesticides through a nematode release system. Lastly, it is suggested that this approach could be applied to other natural systems used for pest control, and that further investigation is necessary to fully explore the implications of this model in real-world scenarios. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the W-shaped network is designed as a nested, bi-directional neural network. On one path, it extracts dense masks from binary masks it has generated, while on the other path, it generates binary masks from the original images. Unlike traditional U-Net based models, which achieve impressive results on nucleus segmentation, but struggle with fused nuclei, this model delivers significantly better performance on this particular challenge. To further enhance its efficacy, the model is trained with a extensive dataset of cancer images containing fused nuclei, along with background noise, and is tested on the notable MSK-ADRIEN dataset, yielding a state-of-the-art error rate of 24.85% for fused nuclei. Moreover, the model's performance is demonstrated across additional datasets containing varied cancer types, along with comparative evaluations against the current state-of-the-art cancer detection algorithms, indicating its superior performance. Additionally, the model's density mask density can be adjusted to meet specific clinical requirements. In addition to its exceptional performance, the model offers a unique advantage - it can be trained on datasets containing point annotations, without having to train it on density mask annotations, thus making it an ideal solution for datasets with limited annotation. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. As the SARS-CoV-2 variant continues to evolve, it is increasingly important to monitor the host-cell response's adjustments, requiring more advanced computational models that incorporate emerging experimental data. As a result, this single-cell model will provide critical host-cell response insights, also enabling discussion on model developments suitable for integrating with the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator. As this simulator receives frequent updates with new experimental data, future directions for this single-cell model will involve incorporating multiple cell types into the research. As such, this model will serve as a precursor for more intricate host-cell dynamics, encompassing the interplay between different cell types in response to various SARS-CoV-2 variants and mutations. As this is a preliminary study, future directions for this single-cell model will involve incorporating several cell types and monitoring the effects of pyroptosis in the broader host-cell context. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. However, the results are sensitive to the choice of parameter values. The proposed approaches could provide a framework for a broader investigation of the effects of the interaction between state and reward variables on reinforcement learning, and might be applied across multiple algorithms. The study's findings could be further optimized, and the proposed methods could be enhanced for real-world scenarios by integrating them with the processes used to preprocess and normalize the state and reward variables in real-world applications. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Furthermore, refined protocols for batch transactions, digital signatures, and public key decryption have been developed and successfully tested with actual Tezos transactions. The development of HELMHOLTZ relies on SMT solvers and refinement types, enabling the detection of errors in Michelson programs with precise messages that can be utilized to improve program debugging. The innovative approach and efficient integration with the refined protocol for transaction validation make HELMHOLTZ a cutting-edge static verification tool for Michelson programs. The project's source code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ai1024/HELMHOLTZ, and Refinement Types for Michelson, the paper on which this article is based, has been accepted for presentation at the 15th Asian Symposium on Programming Languages and Systems (APLAS'17). We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Our research offers a comprehensive, unified explanation of GCNNs and serves as a comprehensive educational material that can be employed as a primer for students to grasp the fundamentals of GCNNs. Additional to the theoretical analysis, a simple implementation in Python using MATLAB's backend for numerical computations is also provided to demonstrate the feasibility of employing GCNNs for image classification tasks. Due to the open nature of this study, we welcome the opportunity for constructive criticism and suggestions to further enhance our understanding of GCNNs. As such, we invite the research community to contribute their own implementations, examples, and educational materials based on our publicly accessible code and framework. All associated content can be found at https://github.com/azay-lebi/Teaching-GCNs. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our coreset's structure enables it to be effectively updated in response to data stream dynamics, thereby supporting continuous $k$-means clustering. Building upon our $k$-means algorithm, we derive a dynamic one-pass algorithm for the $k$-median clustering problem, requiring approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, and subsequently leverage this result to develop a dynamic one-pass algorithm for the $\epsilon$-facility location problem, requiring approximately $\epsilon^{-1}$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$. Additionally, we prove the optimality of our $k$-means algorithm's space complexity through a lower bound demonstration. Lastly, we verify the efficacy of our algorithms through experimental evaluation.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, we observe that the benefit of hierarchical learning increases with increasing complexity of the grid world.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. 

Additionally, our work involves an exploration of 'nontransitive' triples, where the relationship between elements $x_i$ and the likelihood of selecting such a triple, particularly when the lower bound of the range [0,1] is altered, is examined. Our findings demonstrate that the likelihood of choosing a 'nontransitive' triple decreases as the lower limit increases, and that this decrease accelerates when the lower limit is set at 0.5. We have also established upper and lower limits for the likelihood of selecting a 'nontransitive' triple, and that this likelihood approaches a probability of 0 as n increases without bound.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed architecture achieves greater flexibility, enabling the enhancement of various CT images with different doses, such as from low-dose to routine-dose and cancer-radiation dose reduction, without needing to adjust the network architecture. Furthermore, by leveraging the switchable nature of the generator, we developed an intuitive interactive method for patients and radiologists to adjust the dose level according to individual preferences. Our method outperformed state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for low-dose CT image denoising, both subjectively and objectively, and successfully reduced cancer-radiation dose by approximately 12% without compromising diagnostic performance, according to the recently introduced DeepLearning4Medical challenge. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zwang84/SSG-Zhang2023 for replication and further research. The proposed architecture offers a more stable, flexible, and efficient solution for unsupervised low-dose CT image denoising, and can also be applied to other image enhancement applications. The new framework also paves the way for interactive dose adjustment according to individual preferences. The simplified architecture, with reduced memory requirement and weight increase, facilitates the training of deep learning models using limited training data. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. Our research provides a foundation for future video enhancement methods, with possible improvements suggested through analysis of the improved BasicVSR++ model. Our project page can be found at [1].

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. The available code and studies within this research are accessible at the referenced repository.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/owenscase/mbrl-mtrl. Advances

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We further establish that one of these theorems necessarily follows from the combination of the other three results. Additionally, we show that the formulation of first-order logic in the language of peppercorn arithmetic, a formal system introduced by Hagerty in 2009, is capable of deriving the fundamental concepts of arithmetic with the assistance of these theorems. This, in turn, implies that the peccadillo arithmetic is itself capable of deriving the fundamentals of arithmetic. We then explore several other applications of these theorems, including the ability to derive the basic principles of arithmetic within peccadillo arithmetic, and provide new formulations for both theorems and their proofs. Our ultimate goal is to provide a comprehensive foundation for exploring the limitations of formal systems across a broad spectrum of mathematical disciplines. By doing so, we aim to offer a starting point for further research into the fundamental properties governing the relationship between a formal system and its own architecture. This line of inquiry may offer new insights into some of the most fundamental questions surrounding the nature of mathematics and its fundamental principles. This work is intended to serve as a preliminary foundation for a broader theoretical framework dedicated to the study of the axioms and architecture of mathematical logic across a wide spectrum of fundamental mathematical disciplines. This framework is anticipated to facilitate the exploration of core questions concerning the fundamental properties governing the relationship between a formal system and its own architecture, with the ultimate goal of gaining a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles of mathematics itself. This work is meant to be a starting point for further research, rather than a comprehensive survey on the subject. The authors invite feedback, new perspectives, and contributions to this line of inquiry. The theorems discussed herein hold significant implications for our knowledge of the limitations and capabilities of formal systems in mathematics, implying that any consistent, extensionally complete formal system must lack the capacity for self-validation, thereby necessitating a formal system to forgo either consistency or completeness. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Our study's findings provide critical insights into the evaluation of camera calibration using artificial intelligence-based methods. Additionally, we achieved the best results using a simple yet effective approach directly predicting the camera's position from the image, and this approach may serve as a foundation for ongoing research in this area. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Our approach demonstrates the potential to solve complex inverse problems by leveraging the capacity of neural networks to model intricate data distributions, and provides a solution to the problem of evaluating Bayesian inference via generating samples from the posterior distribution. We open-sourced our code and data on GitHub for further research in inverse problems and generative models.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We conclude by discussing the crucial role that invariant manifolds play in the analysis of the behavior of dynamical systems. We also provide examples illustrating the application of these conditions to various systems. Lastly, we discuss potential research avenues related to the topic.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The findings also suggest two screens are linked to specific scintillation patterns observed from different locations on Earth, implying that screens in the solar system's vicinity can be affected by planetary masses. Furthermore, 17 short-term variations in scintillation patterns may be connected to moving small-scale screens, potentially influencing the formation of planetary systems. The results provide direct evidence of small-scale screen movement affecting scintillation patterns and offer a theoretical framework for the origin of voids in the interstellar medium near the solar system. The study's findings validate the idea that studying scattering screens through pulsar scintillation can reveal the interstellar medium's tiny-scale structure and its dynamic processes. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, a subjective quality assessment confirms the capability of QPNet to generate high-quality signals for both known and unknown frequency domains. Furthermore, the model's efficiency is ensured by the reduced number of parameters compared to WN with similar performance. The Quasi-Periodic WaveNet architecture provides valuable insights into designing effective neural networks for modeling signals with complex time-dependent structures and can be applied to other areas where self-similar patterns emerge over relative long periods. This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this interface and present results from
an experiment conducted with the system. We also examine the efficacy of human
annotators with and without the assistance of MADARi, revealing substantial gains
in productivity and accuracy. Furthermore, we explore the potential for using the
system to identify dialects through the analysis of dialect-specific markers, achieving
a classification accuracy of over 80%. We conclude by discussing avenues for
utilizing the annotated corpus, including statistical modeling of dialects and the
development of resources for low-resource languages. We make the MADARi corpus and
the annotation tool itself openly accessible for community utilization and feedback.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. Notably, it differs from other available datasets in several key ways, as it includes a broader range of grades, more comprehensive spectral diversity, and a distinct subset of focal adenomas. By leveraging UniToPatho in our research, we've also demonstrated a notable improvement in a state-of-the-art encoder-based model, resulting in a classification accuracy of 87% and a F1-score of 75% for adenoma grading, and achieved comparable performance in classification tasks. The dataset and corresponding analysis are now available for the medical and computer vision communities to facilitate further advancements in this area.
