A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. As a result, further research is needed to address this limitation. The proposed approach is made accessible through its open-source implementation on GitHub. The associated repository includes an user-friendly interface called Acoustic Scattering Toolbox (AST), offering an intuitive command-line interface for easy implementation and testing of the method. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. 

Furthermore, we found D-poor hydrogen isotopic signatures in the magnesium-rich core fragments of the Chelyabinsk carbonaceous chondrite, which could indicate a D-poor hydrogen rich component in the solar nebula, separate from water. This component might have contributed to the water and hydrogen rich components in the terrestrial planets, separately. 

In addition, our analysis allowed us to evaluate the effects of terrestrial contamination on the previously studied BB-29 and BB-30 samples from the Benenitra chondrite, which showed water content in the range of 0.17-0.33 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O and D-poor isotopic values, indicating minimal contamination. However, we also discovered that the higher water content and D-poor hydrogen isotope values in BB-29 and BB-30 can be explained by a mixture of nebular hydrogen and water with D-values reduced by thermal metamorphism. 

Our research provided new insights into the water and hydrogen isotope composition of chondrite rocks, offering a more detailed view of the formation processes of the solar system and the distribution of volatile elements.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate the benefits of zero-shot learning for speech-to-text in new language pairs. We also observe the advantages of our approaches for languages with limited available data, notably for Vietnamese. To facilitate future research, we release our code, pre-trained models, and data, thereby providing a foundation for the exploration of additional methods in zero-shot speech-to-text. With these developments, we are confident that the field will experience enhanced performance and a broader application spectrum. Our code and resources are available at https://github.com/ghrua/zero-shot-speech-to-text. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues. Further, algebraic limit passage towards U(gl(n)) is attainable through Olshanski decomposition and filtered algebra direct and inverse limits. This research thus extends upon prior works of Lascoux-Leclerc-Schutzenberger, Nazarov-Umeda, Okounkov, and others. For computational purposes, a central Schur element for a given shifted Young tableaux can be calculated via the'standard monomial basis', an actionable outcome of this study. In addition, a central Schur element can be used to induce an 'eigenvalue' on the highest weight vector of an irreducible Schur module, corresponding to a quantum immanant. This study also establishes a direct connection between representation theory and the combinatorial description of shifted Schur numbers, solving shifted Schur problems through representation theory. This research is further illustrated through examples, including the derivation of 'Capelli elements' and 'column Schur elements' and their related quantum immanants, as well as the computation of central Schur elements and their related quantum immanants for specified shifted Young tableaux. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The study also reveals limitations of the relative I-functions' properties when dealing with certain types of singularities. Furthermore, it establishes a direct connection between the relative I-functions and the birational transformations known as Cremona transformations. The results presented may have significant implications for the understanding of the quantum cohomology's behavior under birational transformations. Moreover, they hint at the existence of a fundamental mathematical principle known as the 'hierarchy structure'. This hierarchy structure would govern the relative I-functions and dictate their properties in a way that is both comprehensive and detailed. The study concludes with the prediction that the proposed hierarchy structure will serve as a pivotal foundation for a broader theoretical framework known as the'mirror symmetry'. This proposed framework will then provide a unified and comprehensive understanding of the quantum cohomology, along with its related fields. The study also explores the implications of the proposed hierarchy structure for other mathematical objects related to the quantum cohomology, including the mirror map, the I-functions, and the related hyperplane arrangements. Furthermore, it discusses the role of Cremona transformations within these structures and discusses the quantum cohomology's properties in relation to the birational transformations known as the 'Lefschetz twists'. The study also examines the geometric transition's properties and explores connections with the related mathematical theories of FJRW and the 'extremal transitions'. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The GUI is designed to be user-
friendly, allowing for easy implementation of advanced statistical methods
through simple menu selections, while also accommodating the personalization
of visualization and analysis settings. ViDaExpert is delivered via a user-
friendly GUI built with the Parrot programming language, and is available for
free download from the ISRI website in conjunction with the VidaBase data
format that it uses. The application includes a comprehensive user guide in the
form of a methodically organized HTML document that provides detailed, step-
by-step instructions for using ViDaExpert, along with a brief introduction to
the data format that it employs. The application is compatible with Windows and

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments.
